title: Mechanisms of Acquired Resistance to CDK4/6 Inhibition in Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Adding palbociclib or ribociclib to an aromatase inhibitor or to fulvestrant roughly doubles progression-free survival in hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, yet nearly every tumor eventually resumes growth. The molecular basis of resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition remains poorly defined because paired pre-treatment and progression tissue is rarely obtained. We have assembled a cohort of 340 patients beginning first-line CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy under a protocol mandating baseline biopsy, plasma collection every 8 weeks, and optional biopsy at progression. Preliminary sequencing of 96 progression specimens identified RB1 truncating events, CCNE1 amplification, FGFR1 gain, and PIK3CA and ESR1 substitutions that were undetectable in the matched pre-treatment sample. This proposal will define the frequency, timing, and functional consequence of these lesions and determine whether their appearance in circulating tumor DNA precedes radiographic progression by a clinically useful interval.

Among those first 96 progression specimens, five carried truncating RB1 events accompanied by loss of the remaining allele, seventeen carried CCNE1 copy gain above a normalized coverage ratio of 1.6, and nine carried FGFR1 gain. In thirty-one specimens no alteration absent from the matched baseline could be identified at all, a proportion we regard as informative in its own right rather than as assay failure, since median deduplicated coverage in those specimens exceeded the cohort median. Plasma drawn within 14 days of the progression biopsy recovered 84 percent of the tissue-detected events and, in eleven patients, recovered an event that the single tissue core had missed. These pilot figures fix the event counts, the tissue-to-plasma concordance, and the biopsy capture assumptions on which the power calculations below depend.

The proposal is organized around three properties of each candidate lesion: how often it appears, when it appears relative to the clinical event that ends treatment, and whether its appearance changes what the tumor does. Frequency is estimated from matched tissue pairs sequenced to uniform depth, timing from plasma collected at fixed 8-week intervals from the first dose rather than at clinician discretion, and consequence from a transcriptional output measurement made in the same specimen, so that a copy-number call is never interpreted in isolation from the expression state it is supposed to produce. Lesions that are frequent, that become measurable weeks before imaging changes, and that carry a coherent transcriptional signature are the ones we will nominate for intervention.

We expect to deliver a frequency table for acquired alterations that is free of the ascertainment bias inherent in convenience cohorts, an estimate of the interval between molecular and radiographic escape together with its dispersion across patients, and a prospectively evaluated rule for identifying the patients who should not continue CDK4/6 blockade when the endocrine partner is changed. The cohort, the paired tissue, and approximately 2,400 banked plasma specimens will remain available to the wider field beyond the project period. Sequence data will be deposited under controlled access within 6 months of generation, and analysis code will be released at publication so that frequency estimates can be recomputed under alternative variant-calling thresholds by other groups.

sections.name: Specific Aims
sections.text:
Our central hypothesis is that the alterations recovered from tumors progressing on CDK4/6 inhibition fall into two classes that the existing literature has conflated: lesions that were present before treatment and were merely enriched by it, and lesions that were absent before treatment and were acquired under drug pressure. Only the second class can be dated, and only the second class implies that the tumor changed rather than that the sampling changed. Separating them requires matched baseline material at adequate depth, which is precisely the feature missing from published progression series. Three aims follow from this hypothesis and are pursued within a single, uniformly treated cohort so that the three answers can be joined at the level of the individual patient.

Aim 1 will define the spectrum of alterations that appear during CDK4/6 inhibitor exposure by comparing whole-exome and RNA sequencing of 120 matched pre-treatment and progression biopsies, with prespecified attention to RB1 truncating and copy-number events, CCNE1 amplification, FGFR1 gain, and ESR1 ligand-binding domain substitutions. Exome data will be analyzed for point mutations and for allele-specific copy number, and RNA data will be used to confirm that each copy-number call is accompanied by a transcript change in the expected direction. The prespecified primary comparison is the proportion of progression specimens carrying at least one alteration with zero supporting reads in the matched baseline at a locus covered by at least 100 informative reads. The deliverable is a dated frequency table with exact binomial confidence intervals for each lesion class.

Aim 2 will determine whether these lesions are detectable in serial plasma before imaging changes, applying a 74-gene tumor-informed panel to approximately 2,400 specimens drawn every 8 weeks from 340 participants. Because the panel content is informed by each patient's own tumor, the analysis is not limited to hotspots and can follow copy-number as well as point events. The primary parameter is the lead time between the fitted inflection in variant allele fraction and the date of RECIST progression, estimated with its interquartile range and reported separately for each lesion class. A secondary analysis will ask whether lesions detected only in plasma, and never recovered from the progression core, behave clinically like those confirmed in tissue.

Aim 3 will test, in a prospective sub-study of 90 patients, whether plasma detection of RB1 loss identifies those who derive no further disease control from continued CDK4/6 blockade when the endocrine partner is switched, using a co-primary endpoint of progression-free survival and depth of tumor shrinkage. Assignment is by plasma result rather than by tissue, since tissue is unavailable at the moment the decision must be made. The analysis is prespecified as a comparison between plasma-positive and plasma-negative strata within a single treatment strategy, which addresses whether the marker is informative without requiring a randomization the current evidence would not support.

sections.name: Significance
sections.text:
Endocrine resistance is the dominant clinical problem in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, accounting for most of the 42,000 annual breast cancer deaths in the United States. CDK4/6 inhibitors delay it but do not prevent it: median progression-free survival in the first-line setting is approximately 24 months, and second-line options remain largely empiric. Small retrospective series report RB1 alterations in roughly 5 percent of progression samples and cyclin E1 pathway activation in a further 15 to 20 percent, but these estimates derive from convenience cohorts without matched baselines, so it is unknown which events are selected under drug pressure and which were present all along. A prospectively collected, uniformly treated cohort with dense circulating tumor DNA sampling is required to separate the two possibilities and to prioritize combinations for testing.

The absence of matched baselines is not a minor methodological complaint. A convenience cohort assembled from patients whose disease was accessible to biopsy at progression is enriched for large, superficial, rapidly growing lesions, and the alterations recovered from such lesions may describe the biology of biopsy accessibility as much as the biology of drug escape. Published frequency estimates for RB1 loss in this setting range from 2 to 11 percent across series of fewer than 60 patients, a spread wider than any of the individual confidence intervals, which suggests that between-series differences reflect selection rather than sampling error. Without a baseline specimen from the same patient, an alteration found at progression cannot be assigned to either class, and the entire question of what the drug selects remains unanswerable.

The clinical consequence is visible at every second-line decision. A patient whose disease has progressed after 26 months of an aromatase inhibitor with palbociclib may be offered continued kinase blockade with a changed endocrine partner, a pathway-directed agent, or chemotherapy, and there is at present no measurement that distinguishes among these. Continuation strategies are attractive because they are well tolerated, but if the tumor has lost the substrate on which the drug acts, continuation delivers toxicity without benefit, and the several months spent establishing that will not be recoverable. The interval between molecular and radiographic escape, if it is as long as our pilot suggests, is exactly the interval in which a better-informed decision could be made.

Success would change three things. It would replace the current catalogue of progression-associated alterations with dated frequencies attached to a defined treatment exposure. It would establish whether plasma monitoring at a practical interval delivers a lead time long enough to act on, which determines whether any early-switching strategy is worth testing at scale. And it would provide the first prospective evaluation of a rule for withholding continued CDK4/6 blockade, an intervention that is currently offered on the basis of tolerability rather than evidence of continued dependence. Each of these is a prerequisite for the randomized trials the field will need next, and none can be supplied by further retrospective analysis of tissue collected at progression alone.

sections.name: Innovation
sections.text:
Three features distinguish this proposal. First, biopsy at progression is a protocol requirement rather than an option, and our pilot achieved 71 percent capture, far above the 20 to 30 percent typical of correlative studies. Second, plasma is banked every 8 weeks from treatment start, giving a temporal resolution sufficient to date the appearance of lesions that were absent from the pre-treatment specimen and to estimate the interval between their emergence and imaging change. Third, we couple sequencing to a functional interpretation framework in which each candidate alteration is scored against an eleven-gene E2F transcriptional output signature measured in the same tumor, so that copy-number and transcriptional evidence are integrated rather than reported separately. This design converts a descriptive catalogue into testable, time-resolved hypotheses about how the disease escapes.

The 71 percent capture figure was achieved operationally rather than by exhortation, and the mechanism is transferable. Consent for the progression procedure is obtained at enrollment rather than at the time of progression, when patients are symptomatic and clinicians are focused on the next line of therapy. Interventional radiology slots are held on a standing weekly basis so that the procedure does not compete with diagnostic work, and a research coordinator is paged automatically when a RECIST progression is entered in the trial database. We report these details because the principal reason the field lacks matched pairs is logistical rather than scientific, and a design that solves the logistics is itself a contribution that other groups can adopt.

Fixed-interval plasma sampling from the first dose is the second departure from convention. Most correlative programs sample at baseline and at progression, which yields a before-and-after comparison but no trajectory and therefore no timing information. Sampling every 8 weeks converts each patient into a time series with a median of seven observations, which is enough to fit a change point with a usable standard error. It also permits a question that cross-sectional designs cannot pose at all: whether a lesion that appears early and then plateaus behaves differently from one that appears late and rises steeply, a distinction that may matter more for treatment selection than the identity of the gene involved.

The functional interpretation framework addresses a problem that grows worse as panels grow larger. A progression specimen typically yields several alterations of uncertain consequence, and reporting them as a list invites the reader to assume that each is doing something. By scoring every candidate against a transcriptional output measured in the same specimen, we can say whether a copy-number gain is accompanied by the expression change it is supposed to cause, and we can identify specimens in which the transcriptional state has shifted without any corresponding genomic event. We recognize that this framework will misclassify alterations acting through mechanisms the eleven-gene signature does not report, and we therefore retain the unfiltered variant list as a secondary output rather than discarding it.

sections.name: Approach
sections.text:
Participants receive physician-choice endocrine therapy plus palbociclib or ribociclib on an institutional registry protocol. Baseline and progression cores undergo whole-exome sequencing at 200-fold mean target coverage and RNA sequencing to 40 million paired reads. Plasma undergoes hybrid-capture sequencing at 20,000-fold raw depth with unique molecular identifiers, giving a limit of detection near 0.1 percent variant allele fraction. Variants seen in matched leukocyte DNA are removed before analysis. Timing analyses use a joint model in which plasma variant allele fraction trajectories are fitted as piecewise-linear splines and the change point is compared with the RECIST progression date. With 340 participants and an anticipated 240 progression events we have 84 percent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.60 associated with acquired RB1 loss at a two-sided alpha of 0.05.

Specimen handling is standardized across the three participating sites. Cores are placed in a stabilizing medium within 60 seconds of acquisition, and tumor content is estimated by a study pathologist before library preparation, with specimens below 20 percent tumor content routed to a deeper sequencing protocol rather than excluded, so that low-cellularity lesions are not systematically lost from the frequency estimates. Blood is collected into cell-stabilizing tubes and processed to plasma within 6 hours. Each sequencing batch includes a contrived control with variants titrated at 0.5, 0.2, and 0.1 percent, and a batch is rejected if the expected variants are not recovered at the stated allele fractions. Copy-number calls are made against a rolling panel of at least 96 normal plasma specimens processed on the same platform.

The analytic plan distinguishes three questions and assigns each a prespecified estimator. Frequency of acquisition is estimated as a proportion with exact confidence intervals, with the denominator restricted to loci meeting a depth threshold in the baseline specimen so that absence is not inferred from inadequate coverage. Timing is estimated from the fitted change point of each trajectory, with the interval to radiographic progression summarized as a median with interquartile range and modeled as a function of lesion class. Association with outcome is tested by Cox regression with lesion status entered as a time-dependent covariate, which avoids the immortal time bias that arises when an event detected during follow-up is treated as a baseline characteristic. All time-to-event analyses are prespecified in a statistical analysis plan filed before the first analysis is run.

Several outcomes would complicate interpretation, and we have planned for each. If progression biopsy capture falls below 55 percent, the matched-pair aim will be completed using plasma-defined pairs, with a prespecified sensitivity analysis comparing plasma-only and tissue-confirmed frequencies. If acquired RB1 events prove rarer than the pilot suggests, the outcome analysis in Aim 3 will be pooled across RB1 loss and other events that abolish the transcriptional response, a grouping specified in advance rather than chosen after the counts are known. If the change-point model fails to converge for trajectories with fewer than four positive time points, those patients contribute to frequency but not to timing estimates, and the proportion excluded will be reported. Rigor is supported by blinded variant review, by analysis of sequence data by staff who do not have access to clinical outcomes until the analysis plan is locked, and by independent reprocessing of a 10 percent random sample of specimens by a second laboratory.

title: ESR1 Mutation Dynamics and Next-Generation Oral Endocrine Agents in Advanced Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Activating mutations in the ligand-binding domain of ESR1 arise under the selective pressure of estrogen deprivation and are found in 20 to 40 percent of patients with aromatase inhibitor-exposed metastatic breast cancer. They render the receptor constitutively active, confer endocrine resistance, and are readily measured in circulating tumor DNA. What remains unclear is how these mutations behave over time on treatment, whether specific substitutions differ in their sensitivity to newer oral antiestrogens, and whether treating on the basis of plasma detection improves outcome. This project will characterize ESR1 mutation kinetics in 500 patients sampled every 4 weeks, compare the pharmacology of Y537S, D538G, E380Q, and L536P receptors against fulvestrant, elacestrant, camizestrant, and imlunestrant, and embed a plasma-directed switching strategy within an investigator-initiated randomized trial, NCT03466099.

The three components are deliberately interdependent. The kinetic component defines what a meaningful change in mutant allele fraction looks like against the background of assay and biological variation, which is a prerequisite for setting the trigger used in the trial. The pharmacologic component establishes which agents retain activity against the substitutions most likely to be rising when that trigger fires, which determines what the switch should be to. The trial component then tests the combined strategy against the current standard of waiting for imaging. Each component is individually publishable, but only the combination answers the question a clinician actually faces at the moment a plasma result is returned.

Preliminary work in 84 patients sampled every 4 weeks supports the feasibility of the kinetic aim. Mutant allele fractions in that pilot spanned four orders of magnitude, from 0.05 to 38 percent, and within-patient variation between consecutive draws taken 4 weeks apart during radiographically stable disease had a coefficient of variation of 31 percent, which sets the noise floor against which a rise must be judged. Doubling times estimated from patients with at least five positive draws ranged from 18 to 61 days and differed systematically by substitution. Assay reproducibility across duplicate wells was high, with a concordance correlation coefficient of 0.97 above a fractional abundance of 0.2 percent.

We anticipate three deliverables. The first is a description of how individual ligand-binding domain substitutions behave during aromatase inhibitor and fulvestrant exposure, expressed as growth rates rather than as prevalence at a single time point. The second is a set of concentration-response and receptor half-life measurements for four substitutions across five agents, generated at endogenous expression levels so that the numbers are comparable across compounds and across laboratories. The third is a randomized estimate of whether acting on a confirmed plasma rise before imaging changes prolongs the interval to clinical deterioration. All plasma specimens and all raw sequence data will be made available to investigators outside the project team.

sections.name: Specific Aims
sections.text:
The premise of this proposal is that a plasma mutation result is currently used as a label when it is in fact a measurement with a trajectory. A patient described as ESR1-mutant may have a fraction of 0.06 percent that has been stable for a year or a fraction of 12 percent that has quadrupled in 8 weeks, and these two situations have been treated identically in every trial reported to date. The aims below establish how the measurement behaves over time, what pharmacology the emerging receptor variants actually have, and whether acting on the trajectory changes outcome.

Aim 1 will quantify the temporal behavior of ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations during aromatase inhibitor and fulvestrant therapy using droplet digital PCR for eight recurrent substitutions plus targeted sequencing, in 500 patients sampled every 4 weeks for up to 30 months. The primary parameter is the substitution-specific growth rate estimated from log-linear fits to fractional abundance, adjusted for total cell-free DNA input and normalized to a shared internal control locus. Secondary parameters include the proportion of patients in whom a subdominant substitution overtakes the baseline dominant one, and the concordance between droplet digital PCR and targeted sequencing at the time points where both are performed. The deliverable is a public reference dataset of ligand-binding domain mutation trajectories with linked treatment exposure.

Aim 2 will define substitution-specific pharmacology by expressing each mutant receptor at physiologic levels in ESR1-knockout MCF7 cells and measuring transcriptional output, receptor half-life, and growth inhibition across a concentration range for fulvestrant, elacestrant, camizestrant, imlunestrant, and giredestrant. Every compound is tested in the same cellular background on the same days with shared reference wells, which is the only way to make cross-compound comparisons that the existing literature does not support. Receptor half-life is measured by cycloheximide chase and confirmed by pulse labeling. The prespecified primary readout is the concentration producing half-maximal suppression of transcriptional output, reported with its confidence interval for each of the twenty receptor-compound pairs.

Aim 3 will test in NCT03466099 whether switching endocrine partner at the time of a confirmed rise in mutant allele fraction, rather than at radiographic progression, prolongs the interval to clinical deterioration, with 240 patients randomized 1:1 and a primary endpoint of second progression-free survival. Randomization occurs at enrollment rather than at the time the trigger fires, so that the comparison is between strategies rather than between patients who did and did not experience a rise. Participants in the control arm continue to have plasma drawn, but results are withheld from the treating clinician and the samples are analyzed after database lock, which permits estimation of the lead time that the control arm forfeits.

sections.name: Significance
sections.text:
Endocrine resistance driven by ESR1 mutation is a paradigm of acquired, drug-selected genetic change in a solid tumor. The mutations are rare in untreated primary disease, accumulate in proportion to aromatase inhibitor exposure, and predict inferior outcome when treatment is continued unchanged. Several oral antiestrogens designed to retain activity against mutant receptor have entered late-phase testing, yet the field still selects patients using tissue obtained years earlier or using plasma drawn only at progression. Because mutant allele fractions fluctuate by more than an order of magnitude within a single treatment course, a single time point is a poor guide. Establishing the kinetics, the substitution-specific pharmacology, and the value of acting early on plasma change would convert an established observation into a management strategy.

The pharmacologic gap is as consequential as the kinetic one and is less widely acknowledged. Published potency values for the same compound against the same substitution differ by more than a log unit between laboratories, and the differences track the expression system rather than the compound. Transient overexpression produces receptor concentrations far above physiologic, which saturates the degradation machinery and flattens apparent differences between agents; stable overexpression introduces clonal artifacts that are rarely controlled. A clinician choosing between agents for a patient whose disease carries a specific substitution therefore has no reliable comparative data, and the choice is made on trial eligibility and formulary rather than on receptor pharmacology.

The clinical situation these two gaps produce is unsatisfying in a specific way. Aromatase inhibition acts upstream of a receptor that no longer requires ligand, so its continuation in a patient with a rising mutant fraction is futile in a mechanistically obvious sense, yet the decision to stop is deferred until imaging changes, typically 8 to 12 weeks later, during which the population carrying the substitution continues to expand. Every month of that delay is a month in which the subsequent agent will face a larger and more heterogeneous target. Whether the delay matters is an empirical question that has never been asked in a randomized design.

If the proposal succeeds, three things follow. Plasma monitoring during endocrine therapy would acquire a defined interpretation, with a change threshold calibrated to measured biological and analytic variation rather than chosen by convention. Agent selection at the time of escape would be informed by comparative potency data generated under conditions that permit comparison. And the field would know whether acting on a molecular signal ahead of imaging is worth the additional testing burden, which is the question that determines whether serial plasma monitoring becomes standard care or remains a research activity.

sections.name: Innovation
sections.text:
This proposal treats the plasma mutation profile as a longitudinal signal rather than a static label. Sampling every 4 weeks in 500 patients yields the densest ESR1 time series assembled to date and permits estimation of doubling times for individual substitutions, which we have shown differ by a factor of three in pilot data. The pharmacologic aim uses receptor knock-in at endogenous locus and endogenous expression level rather than overexpression, avoiding the artifact that has made cross-study comparison of mutant sensitivity unreliable. Finally, the embedded randomized trial tests an action, not an association: it asks whether earlier switching helps, which no observational analysis can answer. Together these features move the field from cataloguing mutations toward using their trajectory to time therapy.

The 4-week sampling interval was chosen from the pilot doubling times rather than from convenience. At the fastest observed doubling time of 18 days, an 8-week interval would allow a population to expand more than eightfold between observations, which is enough to miss the inflection entirely; at the slowest, 4-week sampling still yields a detectable change within two intervals. Sampling density is the parameter that determines whether a trajectory can be fitted at all, and it has been set by clinic scheduling in essentially every prior study. Establishing the interval empirically, and reporting what is lost at coarser intervals, is a methodological contribution independent of the biological findings.

The knock-in strategy carries a specific cost that we accept deliberately. Editing the endogenous locus in a receptor-dependent line is slow, yields fewer usable clones than transfection, and requires allele-specific validation of every clone, which is why most groups do not do it. The benefit is that receptor abundance in the edited line remains within the range seen in tumors, so that measurements of degradation depth and receptor half-life are made under conditions where the degradation machinery is not saturated. Because all twenty receptor-compound pairs are measured in the same background, differences between agents can be attributed to the agents.

The embedded trial is the feature that distinguishes this proposal from a natural history study with a good assay. Observational data can establish that a rising mutant fraction precedes progression, and indeed such data already exist, but they cannot establish that acting on the rise is better than waiting, because the patients whose fractions rise differ systematically from those whose do not. Randomizing the strategy rather than the patient population, and withholding plasma results in the control arm while continuing to collect them, produces an unbiased estimate of the benefit of the lead time and simultaneously quantifies how much lead time the standard approach discards.

sections.name: Approach
sections.text:
Plasma is processed within 4 hours into two 4-mL cell-free DNA aliquots. Droplet digital PCR assays for Y537S, Y537N, Y537C, D538G, E380Q, L536P, L536H, and S463P are run in duplicate with a limit of detection of 0.05 percent. Hybrid-capture sequencing of a 61-gene panel is performed at every third time point. Receptor variants are introduced into MCF7 by CRISPR knock-in and validated by allele-specific sequencing. Transcriptional output is measured by RNA sequencing and by a GREB1 and TFF1 reporter. For the trial, 240 patients provide 85 percent power to detect an improvement in second progression-free survival from 6.5 to 10.0 months at a two-sided alpha of 0.05, assuming 20 percent of participants trigger an early switch and a 12 percent dropout rate.

Assay performance is monitored continuously rather than established once. Each run includes a no-template control, a wild-type genomic control at 50 nanograms, and a contrived positive at 0.1 percent fractional abundance; a run is repeated if the wild-type control returns more than one positive droplet or if the contrived positive is not recovered. Because false positives at very low fractional abundance are the principal analytic risk in a monitoring application, a call below 0.2 percent requires confirmation on the second aliquot, and the confirmation requirement is applied identically in both trial arms. Total cell-free DNA input is recorded for every draw and included as a covariate in all trajectory models, since apparent changes in fractional abundance can arise from changes in the wild-type background alone.

Trajectory modeling uses a hierarchical Bayesian formulation in which each patient contributes a substitution-specific growth rate drawn from a substitution-level distribution, with partial pooling across patients. This structure allows rates to be estimated for patients with few positive draws by borrowing strength, while preserving the between-patient variance that a simple pooled fit would discard. The trigger for the trial is defined prospectively as two consecutive draws showing a rise exceeding the upper limit of the measured stable-disease variation, with the second draw at least 4 weeks after the first. Trial analysis is by intention to treat, with second progression-free survival compared by stratified log-rank and a prespecified interim look for futility after 60 events.

The principal risks are enrollment, trigger frequency, and cross-compound comparability. If fewer than the assumed 20 percent of trial participants trigger an early switch, the difference between strategies will be diluted; we will monitor trigger frequency in blinded aggregate at 12 and 24 months and, if it falls below 12 percent, will expand accrual using the reserve provided by our multi-site network rather than relaxing the trigger definition after the fact. If a knock-in clone shows evidence of compensatory adaptation, defined as a shift in baseline transcriptional output greater than twofold from the parental line, it is discarded and replaced from an independently derived clone; all experiments use a minimum of two independent clones per substitution. Rigor is further supported by blinded compound coding in Aim 2, by biological replicates performed on separate days by different operators, and by deposition of all raw droplet-level and sequencing data at publication.

title: Cyclin E1-CDK2 Signaling as a Therapeutic Vulnerability in CDK4/6 Inhibitor-Refractory Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition frequently proceeds through kinase activity that bypasses the drug target entirely. Cyclin E1, encoded by CCNE1, partners with CDK2 to phosphorylate RB1 at sites that palbociclib cannot protect, allowing passage through the restriction point despite full CDK4 and CDK6 occupancy. CCNE1 amplification or transcript elevation is present in 15 to 22 percent of tumors progressing on palbociclib and predicts short duration of benefit when measured before treatment. Selective CDK2 inhibitors have now reached the clinic, but there is no validated way to identify the tumors that depend on this axis, and no preclinical evidence defining the correct sequence or combination. This project will map cyclin E1 dependency across a panel of patient-derived xenografts and organoids, define an expression threshold that separates responders from non-responders, and test CDK2 inhibition alone and with continued CDK4/6 blockade.

The dependency question is not settled by the correlation. Elevated cyclin E1 has been reported alongside palbociclib insensitivity in many datasets, but in most of them the protein was measured by an antibody that does not distinguish full-length from truncated species, and the functional test of whether removing it restores sensitivity was performed in a small number of engineered lines rather than in models carrying the alteration as it arises in patients. Our preliminary data in fourteen patient-derived xenografts show that models matched for CCNE1 copy number differ more than fourfold in cyclin E1 protein and differ correspondingly in palbociclib growth inhibition, which is the observation that motivates a protein-based rather than a copy-number-based selection rule.

The sequencing question is equally unresolved and has immediate practical weight. Both CDK4/6 and CDK2 blockade suppress proliferation of normal marrow progenitors, and our pilot data indicate that concurrent exposure produces a neutrophil nadir substantially lower than either agent alone, at doses that in tumor produce only a modest incremental effect. Whether the additional tumor effect justifies the additional hematologic cost, and whether alternating exposure recovers most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost, cannot be inferred from single-agent data and is a question that preclinical models are well suited to answer before it is asked in patients.

We expect to deliver an isoform-resolved protein measurement with a defined threshold for palbociclib insensitivity, a dependency map across 34 xenografts and 18 organoid lines that other investigators can use to select models, and a direct comparison of concurrent and sequential exposure with tumor and marrow endpoints measured in the same animals. All models generated or characterized in this project will be distributed through our institutional repository, and all growth curves, protein measurements, and phosphosite occupancy data will be released in a machine-readable form at publication rather than as figure panels.

sections.name: Specific Aims
sections.text:
The hypothesis under test is that palbociclib insensitivity in RB1-intact breast cancer is driven by cyclin E1 protein abundance, that the truncated isoforms contribute disproportionately to that abundance, and that the resulting dependency can be reversed pharmacologically without an unacceptable marrow penalty if exposure is scheduled correctly. The three aims correspond to the three clauses of that sentence: measure the dependency, demonstrate its reversibility, and determine the schedule. They are pursued in the same panel of models, so that a model classified as dependent in Aim 1 is the model in which reversibility is tested in Aim 2 and, where derived from a palbociclib-exposed patient, the model carried into the schedule comparison in Aim 3. This continuity is what allows a threshold defined in the first aim to be evaluated as a selection rule rather than merely described.

Aim 1 will measure cyclin E1 protein, including the low-molecular-weight isoforms generated by elastase cleavage, and CCNE1 transcript across 34 hormone receptor-positive patient-derived xenografts and 18 organoid lines, and correlate these with palbociclib growth inhibition. Each model is characterized for RB1 protein, CDKN2A status, and CDK6 abundance so that alternative explanations for insensitivity can be excluded rather than assumed away. The prespecified primary analysis is a receiver operating characteristic comparison of isoform-resolved protein against CCNE1 copy number and against transcript for the discrimination of palbociclib-insensitive models, with insensitivity defined before the protein measurements are made. The deliverable is a threshold with an associated confidence interval rather than a categorical call.

Aim 2 will determine whether CDK2 inhibition restores control of the G1 to S transition in cyclin E1-high models, using PF-07104091 and BLU-222, with readouts of RB1 phosphorylation at serine 780 and serine 807, E2F target transcript abundance, and DNA replication licensing measured by MCM2 chromatin loading. Two structurally distinct inhibitors are used so that any observed effect can be attributed to the target rather than to a compound-specific liability. Genetic confirmation is provided by inducible short hairpin depletion in a subset of six models, and specificity is tested in three cyclin E1-low models where the prediction is that inhibition produces little effect. The deliverable is a quantitative relationship between the depth of serine 807 suppression and the magnitude of growth inhibition across models.

Aim 3 will test sequential versus concurrent CDK2 and CDK4/6 inhibition in eight xenografts derived from patients who progressed on palbociclib, with tumor growth delay as the primary readout and marrow reserve monitored as the principal dose-limiting concern. Four arms are compared: vehicle, palbociclib alone, concurrent combination, and alternating 7-day blocks. Complete blood counts are obtained weekly from the same animals contributing tumor measurements, so that efficacy and toxicity are paired rather than estimated from separate cohorts. A prespecified secondary analysis will express the result as the tumor growth delay achieved per unit of neutrophil suppression, which is the quantity a clinical schedule decision actually turns on.

sections.name: Significance
sections.text:
The clinical failure of CDK4/6 inhibition is not a single phenomenon. Loss of RB1 removes the drug target's substrate and predicts failure of any agent acting upstream, whereas cyclin E1-CDK2 activation leaves RB1 intact and therefore remains addressable. Distinguishing these situations matters because the therapeutic implications are opposite: the first argues for abandoning the pathway, the second for intensifying it. Because CCNE1 amplification and cyclin E1 overexpression are far more common than RB1 loss, the addressable group is the larger one. Establishing a quantitative threshold for cyclin E1 dependency, rather than a categorical amplification call, would allow the first rational assignment of patients to CDK2 inhibitors as these agents move from phase 1 into randomized testing.

Selection matters more for this drug class than for most. Early-phase experience with selective CDK2 inhibitors indicates that dose is limited by myelosuppression at exposures close to those required for target engagement, so a trial that enrolls unselected patients will dilute any true effect while distributing the toxicity across everyone. If the responsive fraction is roughly one in five, as the prevalence of CCNE1 alteration at progression suggests, an unselected randomized trial would need to be several times larger than a selected one to detect the same effect, and the intermediate result of a modestly positive trial in an unselected population would leave the field unable to say who should receive the drug.

A threshold on a continuous protein measurement is also more defensible than an amplification call for a biological reason. Copy number is a discrete property of a genomic segment, but the quantity that phosphorylates RB1 is the protein, and the relationship between the two is loose enough that models with identical copy number differ substantially in kinase output. A categorical call therefore assigns some dependent tumors to the non-dependent group and the reverse, and it does so in a way that cannot be corrected by adjusting the copy-number cutoff, because the error arises between the genome and the protein rather than in the genomic measurement itself.

The schedule question carries independent significance for how this class is developed. The default in oncology combination development is concurrent dosing at the highest tolerated doses of each agent, and departures from that default are usually made after a trial has been stopped for toxicity. Establishing before first combination testing that alternating exposure preserves most of the tumor effect at a substantially lower hematologic cost would let the class be developed on a schedule chosen from evidence. That result would apply beyond this specific pair, since the same logic governs any combination of two agents acting on the same proliferative machinery in tumor and in marrow.

sections.name: Innovation
sections.text:
Most published work has used CCNE1 copy number as a surrogate for cyclin E1 activity. We show in pilot data that copy number explains only 41 percent of the variance in cyclin E1 protein and almost none of the variance in the low-molecular-weight isoforms, which lack the p21 and p27 binding surface and are therefore refractory to endogenous inhibition. Our proposal measures the isoform-resolved protein directly by capillary immunoassay and pairs it with a functional readout of RB1 phosphorylation site occupancy. We also model the sequencing question explicitly rather than assuming that combination is superior; our pilot suggests that concurrent exposure causes disproportionate marrow suppression while sequential exposure preserves efficacy.

Isoform resolution is technically demanding and is the reason this measurement is rarely made. The truncated species differ from full-length protein by a few kilodaltons and are not separated reliably by conventional immunoblotting at the sample sizes available from xenograft tissue. Capillary separation with recombinant standards for each species allows the isoforms to be quantified against a common calibration curve and reported in absolute terms rather than as a ratio to a loading control, which makes measurements comparable across models and across batches. We have established that the assay recovers spiked truncated protein at 92 to 105 percent across the working range, which is the performance required for a threshold to mean anything.

Pairing the protein measurement with phosphosite occupancy addresses the interpretive weakness of any abundance-based marker. Protein can be present without being active, and the quantity that determines whether a cell crosses the restriction point is the phosphorylation state of RB1 at the relevant residues. Parallel reaction monitoring gives site-level occupancy on the same lysate that supplies the protein measurement, so the two can be related within a model rather than across models. This lets us ask whether the abundance threshold works because it predicts phosphorylation, and identify models where it does not, which is where the mechanism is likely to be something else.

Treating schedule as an experimental variable rather than an implementation detail is the conceptual innovation. Combination studies in this field almost always compare a combination against its components and report tumor volume, with hematologic effects noted separately if at all. By measuring efficacy and marrow reserve in the same animals and reporting the ratio, we make the trade-off explicit and testable. The principal risk is that mouse marrow tolerance does not map onto human tolerance, and we address this by expressing schedule effects as relative changes from the single-agent nadir rather than as absolute counts, a form that transfers more reliably across species.

sections.name: Approach
sections.text:
Xenografts are propagated in NSG mice at passage 3 to 6 and authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling. Palbociclib is dosed at 90 mg/kg daily by oral gavage; PF-07104091 at 30 mg/kg twice daily. Cyclin E1 isoforms are resolved on a Simple Western system with recombinant standards. RB1 phosphosite occupancy is quantified by parallel reaction monitoring mass spectrometry. E2F output is summarized as an eleven-transcript score. For Aim 3, eight models with ten mice per arm across four arms give 80 percent power to detect a 40 percent difference in tumor growth delay assuming a coefficient of variation of 0.35. All comparisons use mixed-effects models with model identity as a random effect to avoid pseudoreplication.

Model characterization precedes any treatment experiment and is performed on untreated tumor harvested at a standardized volume of 300 to 500 cubic millimeters, since both protein abundance and phosphosite occupancy vary with tumor size and necrosis. Three independent tumors per model are analyzed and the median is carried forward, with the between-tumor coefficient of variation reported so that models with unstable measurements can be identified rather than silently averaged. Organoid lines are maintained in defined medium without serum, passaged at fixed intervals, and re-authenticated every ten passages. Drug exposure in each model is confirmed by a single terminal plasma concentration in a satellite group, which guards against the possibility that an apparently insensitive model is simply underexposed.

The statistical plan treats the model as the unit of inference for dependency questions and the animal as the unit for schedule questions. For Aim 1, the discrimination analysis is performed across models with bootstrap confidence intervals on the area under the curve and on the threshold, and the threshold is then locked before Aim 2 begins. For Aim 3, tumor volume trajectories are analyzed as log-transformed longitudinal data in a mixed-effects framework with model identity as a random effect, and growth delay is derived from the fitted curves rather than from the last observation, which avoids the bias introduced by differential attrition. Neutrophil nadir is analyzed on the same animals with a repeated-measures model, and the efficacy-per-toxicity ratio is estimated by the delta method with confidence intervals.

Three outcomes would require adjustment. If isoform-resolved protein does not outperform copy number in Aim 1, the threshold aim will report that negative result and Aim 2 will proceed using transcript-defined groups, since the reversibility question stands independently of which marker selects the models. If the two CDK2 inhibitors disagree on any model, that model is flagged and analyzed separately, and genetic depletion is used to adjudicate. If alternating exposure proves inferior rather than comparable, the schedule analysis becomes a negative result of direct clinical value, and the concurrent arm's dose-reduction sub-study becomes the primary route to a tolerable schedule. All animal experiments are randomized by cage after stratification on starting tumor volume, tumor measurements are made by an operator blinded to arm, and group sizes are fixed in advance and reported including animals removed for reasons unrelated to tumor growth.
