title: Adjuvant Abemaciclib and Eradication of Micrometastatic Residual Disease in High-Risk Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Two years of adjuvant abemaciclib added to endocrine therapy reduces invasive recurrence in women with node-positive, high-risk hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, with an absolute benefit of roughly 6 percentage points at five years. Three questions follow. Which patients account for that benefit, given that most would never have recurred? Does the benefit persist after the drug is stopped, or is it deferral rather than eradication? And can the substantial early discontinuation seen in the registration trial, where 17 percent of participants stopped abemaciclib prematurely because of diarrhea, be reduced without diluting efficacy? This cooperative group project addresses all three through a randomized phase 3 trial, NCT05138640, with an embedded circulating tumor DNA program and a prophylactic supportive care intervention.

The three questions are usually pursued separately and by different investigators, which is why they have not been answered. A duration trial without plasma testing can show whether longer treatment helps but cannot say in whom; a plasma correlative study without a duration randomization can identify a high-risk group but cannot say what to do about it; and a supportive care study conducted in a separate population cannot link its findings to efficacy. Combining all three in one protocol costs complexity and buys the ability to relate the mechanistic and the practical results to the same patients.

The deferral-versus-eradication question is the scientific center of the proposal. A curve separation that continues to widen after treatment stops is consistent with elimination of residual disease in a subgroup; a separation that narrows is consistent with suppression during exposure followed by resumption. Extending treatment from two to four years distinguishes these directly, because deferral predicts that the additional two years buy an additional two years of separation while eradication predicts that they buy little. No adjuvant trial in this class has been designed to make that distinction. The distinction is not merely descriptive: it determines whether the correct development path for this class is a fixed course aimed at eradication or an extended low-intensity strategy aimed at suppression.

Expected deliverables are a randomized comparison of two treatment durations with invasive disease-free survival as the endpoint, an assessment of whether early clearance of detectable disease identifies the benefiting group, and a randomized evaluation of prophylactic supportive care measured by completion at intended dose intensity. Plasma specimens and clinical data will be archived through the cooperative group for use by investigators outside the study team. The cooperative group network provides the accrual capacity, the central laboratory, and the long-term follow-up infrastructure required, so the principal risks are willingness to continue treatment for four years and retention through five years of plasma sampling rather than any element of assay performance.

sections.name: Specific Aims
sections.text:
The premise is that adjuvant intensification in this disease is currently conducted without any measurement of the thing it is meant to eliminate. Risk is estimated from the primary tumor, benefit is estimated from population averages, and whether a given woman still harbors disease after treatment is never determined. The aims below add a duration comparison, a direct measurement, and a practical intervention aimed at the largest single reason the treatment is not delivered as intended. Each aim is powered separately, and the factorial structure allows the supportive care question to be answered in the full population without reducing the sample available for the duration comparison.

Aim 1 will randomize 2,400 women with node-positive disease to two years or four years of adjuvant abemaciclib with standard endocrine therapy, with invasive disease-free survival as the primary endpoint, to determine whether extending exposure converts deferral into cure. Randomization occurs at the end of the second year among women still on treatment, which restricts the comparison to those for whom the question is live and avoids attributing to duration any effect of early discontinuation. A prespecified landmark analysis at the end of year four separates the on-treatment and post-treatment periods, since the two durations predict different patterns of separation under the deferral and eradication hypotheses.

Aim 2 will collect plasma at baseline, 6, 12, 24, 36, and 60 months for tumor-informed circulating tumor DNA testing, and will determine whether clearance of detectable disease during the first year identifies the group whose recurrence is prevented. The analysis is prespecified as an interaction between baseline detection status, clearance by 12 months, and treatment assignment, which is the form that would support using the test to select duration. Because detection at baseline is expected in fewer than one in ten women, the aim is powered on the subgroup and reported with appropriate caution about multiplicity.

Aim 3 will randomize participants a second time to prophylactic loperamide plus dietary counseling or to reactive management, with the proportion completing 24 months of abemaciclib at the intended dose intensity as the primary endpoint. The second randomization is orthogonal to the first and occurs at study entry, so that the supportive care comparison spans the whole population and both duration arms. Patient-reported bowel symptoms are collected monthly for the first six months, when most discontinuation occurs, and dose intensity is computed from returned pill counts and pharmacy records rather than from clinician report. A prespecified secondary analysis relates completion at intended dose intensity to invasive disease-free survival, which addresses whether the delivery gap has measurable consequences.

sections.name: Significance
sections.text:
Adjuvant intensification decisions in this disease are made almost blind. Genomic assays estimate the risk of recurrence but say nothing about whether a specific added drug will prevent it, and no assay measures whether micrometastatic disease is still present after treatment. Abemaciclib is expensive, is given for two years, and causes diarrhea in the majority of recipients, so the proportion who stop early is large and the cost per recurrence prevented is high. Identifying the group in whom the drug actually eliminates residual disease, rather than delaying its appearance, would allow the other patients to be spared. Extending the treatment duration is the natural test of whether the benefit is durable.

The arithmetic of adjuvant treatment makes selection unusually valuable here. With an absolute benefit of roughly 6 percentage points, about sixteen women are treated for two years for each recurrence prevented, and the other fifteen receive the toxicity and the cost without any possibility of benefit. Improvements in the drug itself would have to be very large to change that ratio; improvements in selection could change it by an order of magnitude. This is the argument for embedding a direct measurement of residual disease rather than another risk score derived from the primary tumor. It is also the argument for measuring residual disease during treatment rather than only at baseline, since a woman who clears detectable disease and one who never had any are indistinguishable at entry but may differ entirely in what they need next.

The duration question has consequences beyond this drug. If two years of exposure defers rather than eliminates, then the entire adjuvant strategy for this class needs rethinking, and the relevant comparison becomes indefinite low-intensity treatment rather than a fixed course. If it eliminates in a subgroup, then the objective becomes identifying that subgroup and treating them adequately while sparing everyone else. These are opposite conclusions with opposite development programs, and the field currently has no evidence that distinguishes them. Answering it also determines how the next generation of adjuvant trials in this class should be designed, since a deferral mechanism would make invasive disease-free survival at five years a misleading primary endpoint.

The supportive care aim addresses the gap between efficacy and delivery. A drug that is stopped by one in five recipients within the first months cannot deliver its trial-measured benefit in practice, and the gap will be widest in settings with the least support. Because the second randomization runs through a network of 380 sites including community practices, its result will describe the population in which the drug is actually used rather than the selected population of the registration trial. The result will therefore describe the delivery of the treatment as it is actually experienced, which is the quantity that determines the benefit realized at a population level rather than in a protocol.

sections.name: Innovation
sections.text:
This is the first adjuvant CDK4/6 inhibitor trial designed to test duration rather than to test the drug, and the first to embed serial plasma testing as a prespecified mechanistic endpoint rather than an exploratory correlative. The second randomization to prophylactic supportive care is embedded in the same population, which avoids the usual situation in which supportive strategies are tested in separate small studies whose results cannot be linked to efficacy. Because the trial runs through a cooperative group network of 380 sites, the population will include the community setting where premature stopping is most common and where the registration trial had least representation.

The factorial structure is what makes the combination affordable. Randomizing supportive care independently of duration means that the supportive care question is answered with the full sample size rather than with a fraction of it, and that the duration comparison is balanced with respect to supportive strategy. The design assumes no interaction between the two interventions, an assumption we test formally with a prespecified interaction term and report regardless of its significance. Factorial designs are common in cardiovascular trials and rare in oncology, and their absence here has meant that practical and biological questions compete for the same patients.

Prespecifying the plasma analysis as a mechanistic endpoint rather than as exploratory correlative science changes what can be claimed. Exploratory analyses of banked specimens are conducted after the primary result is known, with analysis choices made in light of it, and they generate hypotheses rather than conclusions. Fixing the detection algorithm, the time points, the subgroup definitions, and the interaction test before any outcome data are seen means that a positive result can support a selection strategy directly. It also means that a negative result is informative, which exploratory analyses rarely are. It also permits the plasma result to be reported alongside the primary endpoint rather than years later, which is when a selection strategy would need it.

Conducting the trial through a cooperative group network rather than through academic centers alone is a deliberate choice about generalizability. Early discontinuation is a behavior that depends on the support available, and measuring it in a population supported at academic-trial intensity will understate what happens elsewhere. The trade-off is slower accrual and more heterogeneous data quality, which we address through centralized training, standardized symptom collection instruments, and central monitoring of dose intensity reporting. We also collect symptom data using an instrument administered directly to participants rather than through clinician grading, because clinician-reported gastrointestinal toxicity systematically understates what patients experience and would obscure the effect the supportive care randomization is meant to detect.

sections.name: Approach
sections.text:
Eligibility requires four or more positive nodes, or one to three nodes with grade 3 histology or tumor size of 5 cm or greater. Randomization is stratified by nodal burden, prior chemotherapy, and menopausal status. Plasma testing uses a personalized 32-variant multiplex assay with a limit of detection near 0.01 percent. With 2,400 participants and 340 expected invasive disease-free survival events we have 85 percent power to detect a hazard ratio of 0.72 at a two-sided alpha of 0.05. For the supportive care randomization, 2,400 participants provide over 90 percent power to detect an increase from 78 percent to 87 percent in the proportion completing the intended 24 months at full dose intensity.

Plasma collection is embedded in the visit schedule already required for endocrine therapy monitoring, which is what makes six draws over five years feasible across a large network. Specimens are shipped ambient in stabilizing tubes to a single central laboratory, where processing occurs within 72 hours of draw and time in transit is recorded and used as a quality covariate. Personalized panels are designed from the resected primary using a fixed algorithm, with variants also present in matched leukocyte DNA excluded at the design stage. Detection requires two or more variants above the batch-specific background threshold, and every batch includes contrived positives and negative controls.

The analysis plan handles the three aims separately and controls their multiplicity explicitly. The duration comparison is the primary analysis, using a stratified Cox model with an event-driven final analysis and one prespecified interim look. The plasma aim is a subgroup analysis with a prespecified interaction test, reported with confidence intervals and without claim of confirmatory status. The supportive care comparison uses a chi-square test of the proportion completing at intended dose intensity, with dose intensity defined prospectively as at least 85 percent of planned cumulative dose. Patient-reported outcomes are analyzed as longitudinal ordinal data with a mixed model.

Risks and mitigations are as follows. If the second randomization proves impractical at some sites, participation in that component will be permitted at the site level, with site as a covariate and the resulting reduction in power reported; the duration randomization is not conditional on it. If baseline plasma detection occurs in fewer than 6 percent of participants, the clearance analysis will be pooled with the 12-month detection analysis under a prespecified rule. If accrual to the duration randomization is compromised by unwillingness to continue treatment for four years, the trial will report the proportion declining as a substantive finding about the acceptability of extended therapy. Rigor is supported by central blinded review of invasive disease-free survival events, by laboratory analysis blinded to arm and outcome, by an independent data monitoring committee, and by a statistical analysis plan filed before the first interim analysis.

title: Central Nervous System Dissemination in Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer: Drug Penetration and Tumor Biology

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Brain metastases develop in 10 to 15 percent of women with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, and their incidence is rising as systemic control improves. Most approved agents for this subtype are substrates of P-glycoprotein and breast cancer resistance protein and achieve unbound concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid that are a small fraction of those in plasma. Abemaciclib is a notable exception, with unbound cerebrospinal fluid concentrations approaching those of plasma, and trastuzumab deruxtecan has produced intracranial responses despite its size. This project will measure unbound drug concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid and in resected central nervous system lesions, define the transporter and microenvironmental determinants of penetration, and characterize how the biology of intracranial lesions differs from that of matched extracranial disease.

The rise in incidence is a consequence of success elsewhere. As systemic regimens extend survival by years, patients live long enough for a compartment that was previously a late and uncommon problem to become a common one, and the compartment in question is the one where most systemic agents have never been measured. Registry data from our institution show that the interval from metastatic diagnosis to intracranial involvement has lengthened while the cumulative incidence has risen, which is the pattern expected when a sanctuary site becomes rate-limiting. The consequence is that a compartment historically regarded as a terminal event is now, for many women, the site that determines both survival and the quality of the years that remain.

The central methodological commitment of this proposal is to measure the free concentration in the compartment where the target resides. Total concentrations in tissue homogenate are dominated by binding to lipid and protein and can differ from the free concentration by more than a log unit, in a direction that varies by compound. Reporting total tissue concentration has produced a literature in which agents that cannot engage their target appear adequately delivered and the reverse. Our preliminary measurements in eleven patients show unbound fractions in resected lesion homogenate ranging from 0.008 to 0.21 across the agents proposed.

Expected deliverables are a set of unbound partition coefficients for six agents measured in paired plasma, cerebrospinal fluid, and lesion tissue from the same patients; a determination of whether transporter-mediated efflux is the limiting step for each; and a paired molecular comparison of intracranial and extracranial lesions. All concentration data, sequencing data, and the orthotopic model resources will be shared with the field. The surgical, pharmacologic, and analytical workflows required are established across the participating sites, and the principal risk is accrual of patients undergoing craniotomy while receiving each individual agent rather than any element of measurement. Each agent's partition estimate stands on its own and is reported as it is completed.

sections.name: Specific Aims
sections.text:
The hypothesis is that intracranial failure in this disease has two distinct causes that are usually conflated: for some agents the drug does not reach the compartment at a free concentration sufficient to engage its target, while for others it does and the lesions are nonetheless resistant because their biology differs from that of the extracranial disease on which treatment was selected. The aims measure delivery, identify its determinants, and characterize the biology, so that a given clinical failure can be assigned to one cause or the other. The three aims draw on overlapping patient populations, so that for a subset of participants delivery and biology are characterized in the same lesion, which is the combination that permits a failure to be attributed rather than merely described.

Aim 1 will measure unbound concentrations of palbociclib, ribociclib, abemaciclib and its M2 and M20 metabolites, alpelisib, and deruxtecan in paired cerebrospinal fluid, plasma, and resected brain lesions from 70 patients undergoing craniotomy or ventricular access, using equilibrium dialysis and liquid chromatography tandem mass spectrometry. Dose timing is fixed relative to the procedure so that concentrations are comparable across patients, and the interval between last dose and sampling is recorded and modeled. The primary parameter for each agent is the ratio of unbound lesion to unbound plasma concentration, reported with its dispersion across patients rather than as a single figure.

Aim 2 will define transporter dependence using ABCB1 and ABCG2 knockout mice bearing orthotopic intracranial tumors, and will test whether elacridar co-administration raises intracranial exposure sufficiently to change tumor growth. Both single and combined knockouts are used, since the two transporters have overlapping substrate ranges and a single knockout can be compensated. The efficacy component asks whether a pharmacologic increase in exposure translates into a growth effect, which is the question that determines whether transporter inhibition is worth pursuing clinically rather than merely demonstrable. A prespecified pharmacodynamic component measures target engagement in the intracranial tumor at the exposures achieved, so that a growth effect can be related to whether the target was actually engaged rather than to exposure alone.

Aim 3 will compare paired intracranial and extracranial lesions from 45 patients by exome and transcriptome sequencing, testing the hypothesis that central nervous system lesions are enriched for RB1 loss, CCNE1 gain, and a distinct astrocyte-adapted metabolic program. Pairs are drawn from the same patient within a 90-day window so that differences cannot be attributed to elapsed time on therapy. Cerebrospinal fluid is collected at the same visits and sequenced in parallel, which allows the tissue findings to be related to a sampling method that could be repeated without surgery. The metabolic component of this aim is assessed from transcriptional data with confirmation by targeted metabolite measurement in the subset of lesions where sufficient tissue remains after the concentration measurements.

sections.name: Significance
sections.text:
Central nervous system progression in this population is usually treated as a radiotherapy problem because systemic agents are assumed not to reach the site. That assumption is rarely tested with unbound concentrations in the relevant compartment, and where it has been tested the answer differs sharply between agents that appear pharmacologically similar. Getting this right determines whether a woman with limited brain-only progression should receive whole-brain radiotherapy with its cognitive cost, or a change of systemic agent. Beyond drug delivery, if intracranial lesions carry distinct alterations, then treating them by extrapolation from an extracranial biopsy will systematically mis-assign therapy for the compartment that most limits survival.

The clinical stakes at that decision are asymmetric and long-lasting. Whole-brain radiotherapy produces measurable declines in verbal memory and processing speed within months in a population that may live for years afterward, and the decline is not reversible. A systemic option that controls intracranial disease would defer or avoid that cost. Conversely, choosing a systemic agent that does not reach the compartment wastes the interval in which focal treatment would still have been feasible. The measurement proposed here is the one that separates these choices, and it has not been made for most of the agents in routine use.

The assumption that similar molecules behave similarly is exactly what fails in this compartment. Two kinase inhibitors of comparable size, lipophilicity, and protein binding can differ more than tenfold in free brain exposure because one is an efficient transporter substrate and the other is not, and no property computable from structure predicts this reliably enough to substitute for measurement. This is why the field's practice of extrapolating from one member of a class to another has produced incorrect expectations, and why an agent-by-agent empirical answer is required. Predicting it from physicochemical properties has been attempted repeatedly and has failed often enough that regulators and developers now expect direct measurement, which the breast cancer literature has largely not provided.

The biological half of the proposal matters because delivery is only half the problem. If intracranial lesions are systematically enriched for alterations that abolish the response to a drug class, then adequate delivery will not produce responses, and the correct inference from a failed trial would be about biology rather than about pharmacology. Distinguishing these requires measuring both in the same patients, which is what a craniotomy cohort with paired extracranial tissue uniquely permits. It also determines whether cerebrospinal fluid sampling could substitute for surgery in future studies, which would make the question tractable in the far larger population that never undergoes craniotomy.

sections.name: Innovation
sections.text:
We measure the unbound fraction rather than total concentration, which is the only quantity that predicts target engagement and which is almost never reported for central nervous system compartments in breast cancer. We obtain matched cerebrospinal fluid, plasma, and tumor tissue from the same patient at the same moment, permitting calculation of a true tissue-to-plasma partition rather than a surrogate. The transporter aim uses genetic knockout combined with orthotopic intracranial implantation rather than subcutaneous flank tumors, so the blood-tumor barrier is the physiologically relevant one. Finally, cerebrospinal fluid circulating tumor DNA is collected at the same visits, allowing lesion genotype to be tracked without repeat craniotomy.

Obtaining three matched matrices at a single moment is an operational achievement rather than a technical one, and it is the reason such data do not exist. It requires a neurosurgical service willing to draw cerebrospinal fluid at incision, a pharmacy able to time a dose to a scheduled operation, and tissue handling that freezes the specimen within minutes while the pathologist retains what is needed for diagnosis. We have established this workflow across four surgeons and report the median time from resection to freezing as a quality metric, because unbound concentration measurements degrade rapidly with warm ischemia.

Equilibrium dialysis of tissue homogenate is the methodological core and has a specific pitfall we address explicitly. Homogenization dilutes the tissue and alters binding equilibria, so the measured unbound fraction must be corrected back to undiluted tissue using the dilution factor, a correction that is frequently omitted and that shifts results systematically. We validate the correction for each matrix using compounds of known unbound fraction and report both corrected and uncorrected values so that our numbers can be compared with the existing literature in either form. We also report the free fraction measured in cerebrospinal fluid separately, since protein content there is roughly two orders of magnitude below plasma and the assumption that free and total concentrations are equivalent, though usually reasonable, is not universally so.

Collecting cerebrospinal fluid for tumor DNA at the same visits creates a bridge between the invasive measurement and a repeatable one. If lesion genotype determined from resected tissue agrees with genotype inferred from cerebrospinal fluid in the same patient at the same moment, then the fluid becomes a validated proxy that can be sampled at intervals without surgery. The obvious risk is that shed DNA in this compartment is scarce and that agreement will be limited to patients with leptomeningeal involvement or larger lesions, and we will report agreement stratified by lesion size and leptomeningeal status rather than in aggregate.

sections.name: Approach
sections.text:
Patients undergoing clinically indicated craniotomy receive a timed dose 4 to 8 hours before surgery, with plasma and cerebrospinal fluid drawn at incision. Unbound fractions are determined by rapid equilibrium dialysis at 37 degrees. Orthotopic tumors are established by stereotactic injection of 200,000 cells into the right striatum and monitored by bioluminescence. Elacridar is dosed at 100 mg/kg twice daily. Sequencing of paired lesions uses 250-fold exome coverage with matched leukocyte reference. With 70 patients we can estimate a partition coefficient with a coefficient of variation below 25 percent for each agent, and 45 paired lesion sets provide 80 percent power to detect a difference in the prevalence of RB1 loss from 6 percent to 24 percent.

Analytical methods are validated separately for each matrix, since cerebrospinal fluid, plasma, and brain homogenate differ in matrix effects and in the concentration ranges encountered. Calibration curves span at least three orders of magnitude with stable isotope-labeled internal standards for every analyte, and accuracy and precision are demonstrated at the lower limit of quantification in each matrix before any clinical specimen is run. Non-specific adsorption of the more lipophilic analytes to labware is quantified and controlled by matrix-matched calibrators. For deruxtecan, both conjugated and released payload are measured, since the relevant free species is the released one.

Statistical analysis of the clinical measurements treats each agent separately and reports geometric mean partition coefficients with confidence intervals, modeling the interval since last dose as a covariate to account for the fact that plasma and tissue are not at equilibrium at all sampling times. Between-agent comparisons are made only where the same patients contributed, which the design ensures for patients on combination regimens. The paired lesion analysis compares alteration prevalence within patient by McNemar's test and describes transcriptional differences by paired differential expression with patient as a blocking factor, which removes between-patient variation that would otherwise dominate.

Anticipated difficulties center on accrual, tissue adequacy, and interpretation of negative transporter results. Craniotomy in this population is not common, and we have therefore built the cohort across two additional sites with the same workflow and have prespecified that the primary partition estimates will be reported for any agent reaching 10 evaluable patients, with the remainder described as preliminary. If resected tissue is inadequate for both concentration measurement and sequencing, concentration measurement takes priority and the sequencing aim draws on a separate consented cohort. If knockout mice show no change in exposure for an agent, we will confirm that the assay would have detected a change using a positive control substrate before concluding that the agent is not a substrate. All animal work is randomized and blinded, and analytical runs include quality control samples at three concentrations with prespecified acceptance criteria.

title: A Single-Cell and Spatial Atlas of Endocrine-Resistant Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Bulk sequencing of tumors that have progressed on endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors reports the average of a mixture, and the alterations it recovers explain fewer than half of clinical failures. We propose that much of the missing explanation is not genetic but is carried by transcriptional states occupied by a minority of cells and by the spatial organization of the tumor and its stroma. This center project will construct an atlas of endocrine resistance from 160 paired biopsies taken before treatment and at progression, combining single-cell RNA sequencing, single-nucleus ATAC sequencing, and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics. We will define the states that expand under treatment, relate them to clonal evolution inferred from copy number, and map their spatial relationship to fibroblasts and to cytotoxic T cells.

The averaging problem is not a subtlety of interpretation but a structural feature of the measurement. A population comprising 15 percent of malignant cells with a distinctive program contributes a 15 percent-weighted signal to a bulk profile, which in most tumors falls below the between-patient variation and is therefore invisible. Every published bulk analysis of progression specimens in this disease has been conducted under that constraint, which is a sufficient explanation for why they converge on the same small set of genomic events and disagree about everything else. The consequence is a literature that appears consistent while measuring only the fraction of the biology that survives averaging, and that has little to say about the majority of patients whose failures are not explained genomically.

The paired design is what converts an atlas into an experiment. Comparing progression specimens with baseline specimens from different patients confounds treatment effect with between-patient heterogeneity, which in single-cell breast cancer data is the dominant variance component by a wide margin. Within-patient comparison removes it, and our preliminary analysis of 24 pairs shows that state-abundance changes detectable at n of 24 within patients would require several hundred patients to detect in an unpaired design. The paired design also allows each patient to serve as her own control for tumor purity, dissociation efficiency, and batch, three technical factors that vary far more between patients than within them and that otherwise contaminate abundance comparisons.

Expected deliverables are a paired single-cell and chromatin atlas of 160 biopsies with approximately 250,000 malignant cells, a determination of whether the states that expand under treatment are heritable or plastic, and a spatial map relating those states to stromal and lymphoid neighbors. All data, including raw sequence, cell-level annotations, and spatial coordinates, will be released quarterly through a public portal under a no-embargo policy so that the resource is usable while the project is still running. The biopsy network, the dissociation protocol, and the analysis pipeline are established, and the principal risk is paired specimen yield rather than any element of data generation. Power has been calculated under conservative assumptions about that yield.

sections.name: Specific Aims
sections.text:
The hypothesis is that a substantial share of treatment failure in this disease is carried by transcriptional states rather than by mutations, that these states are occupied by minorities of cells that bulk profiling cannot see, and that their maintenance depends on signals from identifiable neighbors. If the states are plastic, they are targets in the pathway that sustains them; if they are clonally restricted, they are consequences of genetic events and should be addressed as such. The three aims establish which states expand, whether they are heritable, and what surrounds them. The three aims use the same specimens, which means that a state identified in the first can be tested for heritability in the second and located in tissue in the third without introducing between-cohort variation.

Aim 1 will generate paired single-cell transcriptomes from 160 biopsies, targeting 250,000 malignant cells, and will identify transcriptional states whose abundance changes systematically between baseline and progression. States are defined by joint clustering across all specimens with patient effects modeled explicitly, and the primary analysis is the within-patient change in the proportion of malignant cells occupying each state. Because proportions are compositional, an increase in one state necessarily reduces others, and the analysis uses a model that accounts for this rather than testing each state independently. The deliverable is a ranked set of states with effect sizes and false discovery control.

Aim 2 will determine whether these states are heritable or plastic by inferring copy-number-defined clonal structure from the same cells and asking whether state occupancy tracks clonal identity or crosses clonal boundaries. The test is quantitative rather than descriptive: for each state we estimate the mutual information between state assignment and clone assignment and compare it against a null generated by permuting cells within specimen. States that are distributed across clones in most patients are classified as plastic and are the ones for which a pathway-directed intervention is plausible. States that are confined to single lineages are classified as heritable and are interpreted as consequences of the genomic events that define those lineages rather than as independent targets.

Aim 3 will map the states in situ using 960-plex imaging-based spatial transcriptomics on 80 sections, quantifying the distance from each malignant state to CD8-positive T cells, to FAP-positive fibroblasts, and to vasculature, and testing whether resistance-associated states occupy immune-excluded niches enriched for fibroblast-derived FGF and IGF ligands. Distances are compared against a permutation null that preserves tissue geometry and overall cell density, which is essential because any two abundant cell types in a tissue will appear near one another under a naive null. Ligand and receptor transcripts are included in the panel so that candidate signaling relationships can be evaluated rather than assumed from proximity alone.

sections.name: Significance
sections.text:
Resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition and to endocrine therapy is currently explained genetically in only 40 to 50 percent of cases, and the remaining patients receive treatment chosen without any mechanistic basis. If a substantial share of failures is driven by reversible transcriptional states rather than by fixed mutations, then the therapeutic strategy changes entirely: the target becomes the pathway maintaining the state, and the timing becomes early, before the state is established. Spatial context matters because an identical transcriptional state may be sustained by a fibroblast-derived ligand in one region and be immunologically constrained in another. An atlas at this resolution provides the reference against which mechanistic and therapeutic hypotheses can be tested.

The unexplained half of the problem is not a minor residual. In practical terms it means that for roughly one in two patients whose disease escapes, a full genomic report returns nothing that directs the next treatment, and the choice is made from a menu ordered by tolerability and habit. That situation has been stable for a decade despite steadily broader sequencing panels, which is itself evidence that the missing explanation is not a rarer mutation waiting to be found by a larger panel. The consequence for patients is that the choice made at progression is effectively arbitrary for half of them, and the consequence for the field is that trials in this setting enroll populations whose biology is unknown at entry.

The distinction between heritable and plastic states has direct therapeutic consequences that are often left implicit. A genetically fixed subclone can only be eliminated, and eliminating it requires an agent to which it is sensitive; a plastic state can in principle be prevented or reversed, and preventing it requires acting before it is established, which means during the response rather than at progression. These imply different trial designs, different endpoints, and different combination partners, and the field currently pursues both without knowing which applies. Establishing which applies for the states that actually expand under treatment is therefore not a refinement but a precondition for designing the next generation of combination trials.

Spatial organization is the element most likely to be underestimated. Two tumors with identical state composition can differ entirely in whether those states are adjacent to fibroblasts producing growth factors or to lymphocytes capable of killing them, and that difference determines whether an intervention against the supporting signal or against the immune constraint is the right one. Measuring composition without geometry has been the standard because the technology was not available; it now is, and the resulting maps are the reference the field lacks. An atlas also has value beyond the specific hypotheses tested here, since the same specimens and annotations can be interrogated by other groups against questions we have not anticipated.

sections.name: Innovation
sections.text:
The design is paired within patient, which removes the between-patient variance that dominates existing single-cell breast cancer datasets and which has made state-abundance comparisons underpowered. We integrate chromatin accessibility from the same specimens, allowing us to ask whether an expanded state carries a stably remodeled regulatory landscape or a transient transcriptional program. The joint inference of clonal structure and transcriptional state from the same cells is unusual and directly addresses the heritability question that determines whether the state is a target or a symptom. All data, including raw sequence, cell-level annotations, and spatial coordinates, are released quarterly through a public portal under a no-embargo policy.

Obtaining 160 paired biopsies of adequate quality is the principal barrier and the principal contribution. Luminal breast epithelium dissociates poorly and is disproportionately lost with standard warm protocols, so a naive single-cell dataset from this disease is enriched for immune and stromal cells and depleted of exactly the malignant populations of interest. Our cold-active protease protocol was developed to address this and recovers malignant fractions two to three times higher than warm dissociation in side-by-side comparison, which is what makes a target of 250,000 malignant cells achievable from core biopsies. We report the malignant fraction recovered for every specimen so that the effect of the protocol can be judged rather than asserted.

Adding chromatin accessibility from the same specimens converts a descriptive observation into a mechanistic one. A transcriptional state accompanied by remodeled accessibility at the corresponding motifs is more likely to be stably maintained and to require an intervention against the factor driving it; a state visible only in transcript is more likely to be a transient response that will revert when the pressure is removed. This distinction cannot be made from expression alone, and making it in the same specimens rather than in a separate cohort avoids attributing to biology what may be a difference between cohorts.

The no-embargo release policy is a deliberate design decision with a cost. Quarterly public release means that other groups may publish analyses of our data before we do, and we accept that because a reference atlas is only useful if it is available while questions are being asked. The corresponding risk is that early releases contain annotations that are later revised, and we address this by versioning every release, retaining prior versions, and documenting changes so that analyses can be reproduced against the version on which they were performed. We also publish the analysis code alongside each release, so that a user can determine exactly how a given annotation was produced.

sections.name: Approach
sections.text:
Biopsies are collected on ice and dissociated within 30 minutes using a cold-active protease protocol that preserves fragile luminal epithelium. Single-cell libraries are prepared to a target of 5,000 cells per sample at 50,000 reads per cell. Chromatin accessibility uses a droplet single-nucleus protocol on cryopreserved nuclei. Copy number is inferred with a hidden Markov model over 10-megabase bins, benchmarked against matched exome data. Spatial data are segmented with a nuclear expansion model and validated against immunofluorescence for a nine-marker subset. State abundance changes are tested with a Dirichlet-multinomial mixed model, which controls the compositional false-positive rate that has affected earlier reports. Power simulations indicate detection of a twofold change in a state comprising 4 percent of cells at 80 percent power.

Specimen flow is standardized to keep the paired structure intact. Each biopsy yields cores allocated in a fixed order to fresh dissociation, to cryopreservation for nuclei, and to formalin fixation for spatial analysis, so that a specimen that fails one assay still contributes to the others and the reason for failure is recorded. Baseline and progression specimens from the same patient are processed in the same batch wherever the interval permits, and where it does not, batch is included as a covariate and a set of reference specimens is included in every batch to permit correction. Dissociation-induced stress signatures are quantified in every specimen and used to exclude cells rather than whole samples.

Analysis proceeds in a fixed order with decisions locked before the next step. States are defined once, from a joint embedding across all specimens with patient modeled as a random effect, and the state definitions are frozen before any abundance testing. Copy-number inference is benchmarked against matched exome data in a subset and the concordance reported before clonal assignments are used. Spatial analyses use a permutation null preserving tissue geometry, and all distance comparisons are reported with the null distribution rather than only a p value. Multiplicity across states is controlled at a 5 percent false discovery rate within each aim.

The main risks are specimen attrition, state instability, and segmentation error. If paired specimen yield falls below 120 pairs, power simulations indicate detection of a twofold change in a state comprising 6 rather than 4 percent of cells, and we will report the revised detection limit rather than reinterpret the threshold post hoc. If states defined in the discovery half of the cohort do not replicate in the held-out half, they will be reported as non-replicating; we have prespecified a split-sample validation for exactly this purpose. If spatial segmentation proves unreliable in regions of high cell density, distance analyses will be restricted to regions passing a prespecified quality metric, with the excluded fraction reported. Rigor is supported by processing and analysis staff blinded to specimen timepoint where feasible, by inclusion of reference specimens across batches, and by public release of code alongside data.

title: Targeted Degradation of the Estrogen Receptor and Cyclin-Dependent Kinases in Endocrine-Resistant Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Fulvestrant, the only approved selective estrogen receptor degrader, removes 40 to 60 percent of receptor protein at achievable exposures and is limited by poor oral bioavailability. Heterobifunctional degraders recruit an E3 ubiquitin ligase to the target and act catalytically, achieving deeper and more sustained loss of protein. Vepdegestrant, a cereblon-recruiting estrogen receptor degrader, eliminates more than 90 percent of receptor at low nanomolar concentrations, including receptor carrying the Y537S substitution that confers endocrine resistance. This project extends targeted protein degradation from the receptor to the kinases downstream of it. We will optimize CDK4-selective and CDK6-selective degraders, determine whether removing the kinase protein rather than inhibiting its catalytic site produces a deeper and more durable arrest, and define the combination behavior of receptor and kinase degraders.

The rationale for moving from the receptor to the kinases is not simply that the chemistry is available. CDK4 and CDK6 are highly similar in their catalytic pockets and are consequently inhibited together by every approved agent in the class, so their individual contributions to therapeutic effect and to toxicity have never been separated in a tumor. Their roles are known to diverge outside the catalytic function, and the hematologic toxicity that limits the class is attributed disproportionately to one of them. A selective removal strategy is therefore both a mechanistic tool and a potential therapeutic advantage.

Our preliminary chemistry supports the feasibility of that selectivity. From an arrayed screen of ligase-recruiting ligands paired with a common kinase-binding warhead, we have identified lead compounds that deplete one kinase substantially more than the other, and the selectivity arises from differences in ternary complex geometry rather than from differences in warhead affinity, which is why it is achievable by degradation and not by inhibition. Proteome-wide profiling of these leads shows no other protein depleted by more than 30 percent at the working concentration. Selectivity of this kind is also verifiable in a way that inhibitor selectivity often is not, since the readout is the abundance of every protein in the proteome rather than inhibition of a preselected kinase panel.

Expected deliverables are a characterized set of selective kinase degraders with measured proteome-wide selectivity, a direct comparison of removal against catalytic inhibition in models with and without prior drug exposure, and combination data for receptor and kinase degraders in models derived from treated patients. All compounds will be made available to academic investigators, and all degradation, selectivity, and efficacy data will be released in machine-readable form. The chemistry, the tagged cellular systems, and the models derived from treated patients are all established, so the project begins with characterization rather than with discovery. Each aim produces an interpretable result independent of the others, and the combination aim is designed to be informative whether or not it favors the degraders.

sections.name: Specific Aims
sections.text:
The hypothesis is that removal of a target protein differs from inhibition of its catalytic site in ways that matter therapeutically in this disease: removal is catalytic and therefore achieves depth that occupancy cannot, it outlasts plasma exposure, it is less sensitive to substitutions that reduce ligand affinity, and it eliminates functions that do not depend on catalysis. The three aims test each of these claims for the receptor, extend the approach to the kinases, and evaluate the combination. The aims are sequenced so that the receptor comparison, where the chemistry is most mature, establishes the measurement framework subsequently applied to the kinase compounds.

Aim 1 will compare vepdegestrant with fulvestrant across a panel of ESR1 genotypes, including wild type, Y537S, Y537N, D538G, and E380Q, measuring degradation half-maximal concentration, receptor half-life, and suppression of GREB1 and TFF1 transcription in knock-in MCF7 and T47D cells and in six xenografts. All genotypes are compared in the same cellular background with the receptor expressed from its endogenous locus, which is what makes the potency values comparable across genotypes. A prespecified secondary analysis measures the persistence of receptor loss after washout, since the duration of effect after exposure falls is the property most likely to differ between the two mechanisms.

Aim 2 will develop and characterize CDK4-selective and CDK6-selective degraders based on cereblon and von Hippel-Lindau ligands, defining selectivity by whole-proteome mass spectrometry across 8,500 quantified proteins. Selectivity is characterized at three concentrations spanning the working range rather than at a single one, because degrader selectivity typically narrows as concentration rises and a single-point measurement can be misleading. Ternary complex formation is measured biophysically for each lead so that the structural basis of selectivity can be related to the cellular result, and compounds are advanced only after both cellular and proteomic criteria are met. The deliverable is a matched pair of tool compounds with documented selectivity, suitable for distribution to other laboratories investigating the separate roles of the two kinases.

Aim 3 will test receptor plus kinase degrader combinations against palbociclib-containing regimens in eight xenografts derived from patients with prior CDK4/6 inhibitor exposure, with depth and duration of tumor regression as endpoints. Models are characterized for RB1 protein before treatment, since removal of an upstream protein cannot restore a downstream function that is absent, and this characterization is used to interpret rather than to select. The comparison includes a palbociclib plus fulvestrant arm representing current practice, so that the result is expressed relative to what a patient would otherwise receive. A prespecified pharmacodynamic sub-study measures target abundance in tumor at intervals after the last dose, which tests directly whether the duration of effect exceeds the duration of exposure.

sections.name: Significance
sections.text:
Every approved agent in this disease acts by occupancy: the drug must remain bound to block function, and mutations that reduce affinity restore signaling. Degradation acts by removal, so a single degrader molecule can eliminate many target molecules and the pharmacodynamic effect outlives the plasma exposure. This distinction matters most where occupancy is failing, which is precisely the setting of endocrine resistance. Extending the approach to CDK4 and CDK6 addresses a second limitation: kinase inhibitors leave scaffold functions intact, and both kinases have catalytically independent roles in transcriptional regulation and in the DNA damage response. Removing the protein tests whether those scaffold functions contribute to incomplete responses.

The clinical problem this addresses is the shallowness of response in a disease that is otherwise well controlled. Patients on endocrine therapy with a kinase inhibitor typically achieve stabilization or modest shrinkage rather than deep regression, and disease that has been stabilized for two years resumes growth within weeks of stopping treatment. Both observations are consistent with substantial residual target function, which is what occupancy-based blockade at achievable exposures produces. Whether deeper removal converts stabilization into regression is a question that could not be asked until compounds capable of that depth existed. Establishing whether it does would also clarify how much of the observed clinical benefit reflects incomplete blockade rather than intrinsic limits of the target.

Separating the two kinases would answer a question that has been unanswerable since the class was developed. Because every clinical agent inhibits both, the field cannot say whether the antitumor effect requires both, whether the neutropenia that limits dosing is attributable predominantly to one, or whether a selective agent would have a wider therapeutic index. These are not academic questions: the dose intensity actually delivered to patients is set by hematologic toxicity, and an agent that spared the responsible kinase could be given at exposures that the current class cannot reach. Answering these questions requires tools that discriminate between the two proteins in a living tumor, which is exactly what the compounds proposed here provide.

Finally, the scaffold argument generalizes beyond this pair. If removal proves superior to inhibition in a setting where the catalytic function has been thoroughly targeted for a decade, that result is evidence that non-catalytic functions matter for kinases generally, which bears on target selection across oncology. If removal proves equivalent, that is also worth knowing, because it would indicate that the additional complexity of degrader development is not justified for well-inhibited targets. That negative result would be equally useful in directing effort, since degrader campaigns consume substantially more medicinal chemistry resource than inhibitor campaigns against the same target.

sections.name: Innovation
sections.text:
Selective removal of CDK4 without CDK6, or the reverse, is not achievable pharmacologically because the ATP pockets are nearly identical, but it is achievable through degradation because ternary complex formation depends on surfaces distant from the pocket. Our lead compounds show 40-fold selectivity between the two, which allows the first clean test of their separate contributions in a tumor. We also apply degrader chemistry to a target-and-ligase pairing chosen from an arrayed screen of 96 ligase-recruiting ligands rather than from the two ligases used by convention, which broadens the tissue-selectivity options. Proteome-wide selectivity is measured for every compound before biological interpretation, a standard rarely met in this literature.

Achieving selectivity through complex geometry rather than through binding affinity is the conceptual advance, and it inverts the usual constraint of medicinal chemistry. A warhead that binds both proteins equally can nonetheless produce selective degradation if only one of the resulting ternary complexes is productive, which means that selectivity can be engineered into the linker and the ligase ligand rather than into the target-binding element. This decouples selectivity from affinity and opens targets that were considered undruggable by selectivity criteria. It also means that selectivity must be demonstrated empirically for each compound rather than predicted, which is why proteome-wide profiling is built into the advancement criteria rather than performed at the end.

Screening ligase ligands in an arrayed format rather than defaulting to the two conventional ligases addresses a practical limitation of the field. E3 ligase expression varies substantially between tissues, and a degrader built on a ligase that is abundant in marrow will deplete its target in marrow, which is precisely where the class's toxicity lies. Screening across 96 recruiting ligands gives options for pairing a target with a ligase whose expression pattern favors tumor over the dose-limiting tissue, which is a route to therapeutic index that inhibitor chemistry does not offer. We characterize expression of the recruited ligase in marrow progenitors alongside tumor for every advanced compound, so that the pairing can be selected on evidence.

Requiring proteome-wide selectivity data before biological interpretation is a standard rather than a technique, and we adopt it because the alternative has produced a literature that is difficult to trust. A degrader that depletes several unintended proteins will produce phenotypes that are attributed to the intended target, and the attribution is rarely tested. Measuring 8,500 proteins at three concentrations for every advanced compound is expensive and slow, and it is the reason our compound advancement rate will look modest relative to programs that omit it. We regard that as the correct trade, because a tool compound with undocumented off-target activity produces conclusions that must later be retracted.

sections.name: Approach
sections.text:
Degradation is quantified by HiBiT-tagged endogenous alleles read every 15 minutes over 24 hours, with half-maximal degradation concentration and maximum degradation fitted from four-parameter curves. Ternary complex formation is measured by time-resolved fluorescence energy transfer and by surface plasmon resonance. Whole-proteome selectivity uses tandem mass tag labeling with 8,500 proteins quantified at 1 percent false discovery rate. Xenografts derived from patients previously exposed to palbociclib are propagated at passage 3 to 5 in NSG mice, with eight animals per arm. Depth of regression is analyzed as best percentage change from baseline volume and duration as time to a doubling of nadir volume, using mixed-effects models with model identity as a random effect.

Cellular systems are constructed to remove the artifacts that make degrader potency values incomparable between laboratories. Tags are knocked in at the endogenous locus so that target abundance is unaltered, and tagged lines are verified against parental lines for growth rate, target abundance by orthogonal immunoassay, and drug sensitivity. Every degradation experiment includes a ligase-knockout control and a competition arm with excess ligase ligand, both of which must show loss of degradation for the result to be accepted. Compounds are assayed at matched free concentration, with protein binding in the assay medium measured rather than assumed, because differences in serum binding between compounds otherwise masquerade as differences in potency.

The in vivo analysis is designed around the two properties that distinguish degraders from inhibitors. Depth is captured by best percentage change from baseline, analyzed as a continuous outcome rather than dichotomized into response categories, which preserves information in a setting where most agents produce stabilization. Duration is captured by time to a doubling of nadir volume, analyzed by mixed-effects Cox regression with model identity as a random effect. Pharmacodynamic sampling in satellite animals at 4, 24, and 72 hours after the final dose establishes whether target loss persists after exposure has fallen, which is the mechanistic claim that the efficacy comparison is meant to test.

Three contingencies are planned. If the selective kinase degraders lose selectivity in vivo, which can occur through metabolite formation, we will characterize the principal metabolites and, if necessary, advance a backup series from the arrayed screen rather than reinterpret the in vivo result. If models derived from palbociclib-exposed patients prove uniformly RB1-deficient, the combination aim will be supplemented with models from patients with shorter prior exposure, since the question concerns the setting where a downstream brake remains. If proteome-wide profiling identifies an off-target depletion that cannot be engineered out, the affected compound will be retained as a tool with the caveat stated rather than presented as selective. All animal studies are randomized by cage with blinded measurement, and all compound characterization is performed on at least two independently synthesized batches.

title: Integrated Genomic and Transcriptomic Landscape of Endocrine-Resistant Metastatic Hormone Receptor-Positive Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
We performed whole-exome and RNA sequencing on 212 metastatic biopsies from patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer who had progressed on at least one line of endocrine therapy, with matched primary tumors available for 96. ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations were present in 21.2 percent of metastases and in none of the matched primaries, establishing them as acquired under treatment. PIK3CA mutations occurred in 38.2 percent, ERBB2 activating mutations in 4.2 percent, NF1 loss-of-function events in 6.6 percent, and RB1 biallelic inactivation in 4.7 percent. Transcriptional analysis identified a subgroup with elevated E2F and MYC target expression despite intact RB1. Clonal evolution analysis of matched pairs showed that endocrine resistance is usually driven by lesions that expanded from minor populations rather than by lesions present in the dominant primary clone.

The cohort was assembled prospectively rather than from archived material, with biopsy performed at the moment of documented progression and with matched leukocyte DNA available for every participant. Median age at metastatic biopsy was 58 years, median number of prior endocrine lines was two, and 71.2 percent had received an aromatase inhibitor for at least 12 months. Biopsy sites were liver in 41 percent, bone in 24 percent, lymph node in 19 percent, and other soft tissue in 16 percent, and the distribution of recovered alterations did not differ materially by site once tumor content was accounted for. Median tumor content was 44 percent, and specimens below 20 percent were sequenced more deeply rather than excluded.

Beyond the individual gene frequencies, two structural findings emerged. Alterations differed systematically in their clonal position: PIK3CA mutations were carried by the dominant population and shared with the matched primary, whereas ESR1 and RB1 events were subclonal in the primary when detectable at all. And a substantial group of tumors with no recovered driver of endocrine resistance nonetheless showed a coherent transcriptional phenotype, indicating that the exome does not capture the whole of the problem. Together these observations argue that resistance in this disease is assembled from pre-existing and selected components in proportions that differ by gene.

The clinical implication is that the alteration list obtained from an archival primary tumor is a poor guide to the state of metastatic disease, since the alterations most relevant to the next treatment decision are precisely those least likely to be represented in it. A metastatic specimen obtained at progression recovers the acquired events; a primary specimen does not. Because rebiopsy is not always feasible, this finding also motivates the development of blood-based approaches that can recover the same information repeatedly, a direction we pursue in companion work.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text:
Approximately three quarters of breast cancers express the estrogen receptor, and essentially all metastatic disease in this group eventually becomes refractory to estrogen deprivation. The genomic basis of that transition has been studied largely in primary tumors, which are removed before the selective pressure of endocrine therapy has been applied and which therefore cannot show what that pressure selects. Reports from small metastatic series have implicated ESR1 mutation, PI3K/AKT pathway activation, and loss of RB1, but the relative frequency of these events, their clonal relationship to the primary tumor, and their transcriptional consequences have not been assessed together in a single cohort. We assembled a prospectively biopsied metastatic cohort with paired primary tissue in order to distinguish selected alterations from pre-existing ones.

The distinction matters for interpretation as much as for treatment. An alteration observed in a metastatic specimen may have been present in the primary tumor at a frequency below detection, may have arisen after dissemination, or may have been present all along in the population that seeded the metastasis. These histories have different implications: the first and third suggest that the alteration was permitted rather than selected, while the second implicates the treatment. Without matched primary tissue and without clonal reconstruction, all three appear identical, which is why frequency tables derived from metastatic specimens alone have been difficult to interpret.

Transcriptional characterization has been still less complete. Most metastatic sequencing efforts have been exome-only, on the reasonable grounds that RNA from core biopsies is variable in quality and that the actionable findings are mutational. But the pathways of interest here are ones whose activity can change without a mutation, and a tumor that has restored proliferative signaling through transcriptional rather than genomic means will appear driverless on an exome. Adding RNA sequencing to the same specimens allows the two kinds of explanation to be compared within the same tumor rather than across studies.

We therefore designed this study around three requirements: prospective biopsy at the moment of clinical progression rather than retrieval of whatever archival material existed, matched primary tissue and matched leukocyte DNA for as many participants as possible, and paired exome and transcriptome data from the same specimen. The resulting cohort of 212 metastatic biopsies, with matched primaries for 96, is to our knowledge the largest in which all three conditions are met, and it permits the frequency, the clonal position, and the transcriptional consequence of each alteration to be reported together.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text:
Patients underwent image-guided core biopsy of a metastatic lesion at the time of clinical progression between 2012 and 2016. Exome libraries were sequenced to 220-fold mean target coverage for tumor and 90-fold for matched peripheral blood leukocyte DNA. Somatic calling used a consensus of three callers with a minimum of five supporting reads and a variant allele fraction of at least 4 percent. Variants also present in matched leukocyte DNA were removed from the somatic set and analyzed separately; pathogenic BRCA2 and PALB2 variants identified in that fraction were present in 6.2 percent of patients. RNA libraries were sequenced to 45 million paired reads. Clonal structure was reconstructed with a Dirichlet process model over copy-number-corrected variant allele fractions, and phylogenies were inferred for the 96 matched pairs.

Eligibility required histologically confirmed hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative disease, radiographic progression on at least one line of endocrine therapy, and a lesion accessible to core biopsy without unacceptable risk. Between two and four cores were obtained per procedure, with one core reserved for pathology review and the remainder allocated in a fixed order to nucleic acid extraction. Tumor content was estimated on a hematoxylin and eosin section by a study pathologist blinded to the sequencing result. Procedures were performed by a small group of interventional radiologists using a common protocol, and complication rates were recorded prospectively; no procedure resulted in a grade 3 or higher adverse event.

Copy number was derived from the exome data using a log-ratio segmentation approach with allele-specific information from heterozygous sites, calibrated against tumor content and ploidy estimated jointly from the variant allele fraction distribution. Biallelic inactivation was called when a truncating or clearly deleterious variant coincided with loss of the remaining allele, or when both alleles carried independent deleterious variants; single-copy loss without a second event was recorded separately. Transcript-level quantification used a transcriptome-aware aligner with normalization to upper quartile counts, and specimens with fewer than 20 million uniquely mapping reads or with a degradation metric below threshold were excluded from expression analyses.

Statistical analyses were prespecified where the analysis addressed a stated hypothesis and are labeled as exploratory otherwise. Frequencies are reported with exact binomial confidence intervals. The association between exposure duration and ESR1 mutation frequency was tested by the Cochran-Armitage trend test across prespecified exposure strata. Time to subsequent progression was analyzed by Cox regression adjusted for line of therapy, visceral involvement, and biopsy site, with proportional hazards verified by scaled Schoenfeld residuals. Multiple comparisons across genes were controlled at a 10 percent false discovery rate. All patients provided written informed consent under an institutional review board-approved protocol.

sections.name: Results
sections.text:
ESR1 mutations were confined to aromatase inhibitor-exposed patients and rose in frequency with duration of exposure, from 6.9 percent below 12 months to 34.1 percent above 36 months. Y537S and D538G accounted for 71 percent of ESR1 events. PIK3CA mutations were largely clonal and shared with the matched primary, consistent with an early event. RB1 inactivation was always subclonal in the primary when detectable at all and clonal in the metastasis. Tumors with intact RB1 but high E2F output showed elevated CCNE1 and CDK6 transcript levels and shorter time to subsequent progression, with a median of 4.1 versus 9.8 months and a hazard ratio of 1.94 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.31 to 2.87.

Of the 212 metastatic specimens, 208 yielded exome data meeting quality thresholds and 187 yielded usable transcriptomes. Median somatic mutation burden was 2.9 per megabase, with 11 specimens above 10 per megabase, of which 6 carried a mismatch repair gene alteration. The trend in ESR1 frequency with exposure duration was significant at p below 0.001, and no ESR1 ligand-binding domain event was observed among the 34 patients whose only prior endocrine therapy was tamoxifen. Among the 45 ESR1-mutant specimens, 17 carried more than one distinct substitution, and in 11 of these the substitutions were assigned to separate clonal lineages by the reconstruction.

Clonal analysis of the 96 matched pairs showed that 82 percent of the alterations distinguishing metastasis from primary were carried by populations inferred to have been present at low frequency in the primary rather than acquired de novo, although the resolution of the primary sequencing does not permit this to be established for any individual variant. NF1 loss-of-function events, present in 6.6 percent, were enriched among patients with three or more prior endocrine lines, at 12.1 versus 3.8 percent. ERBB2 activating mutations were mutually exclusive with ESR1 events in this cohort, with no specimen carrying both, although the small numbers preclude a firm conclusion.

The RB1-intact, E2F-high group comprised 31 specimens, 16.6 percent of those with transcriptome data, and was defined by an output score in the top quartile in the absence of any RB1 alteration. This group did not differ from the remainder in ESR1 or PIK3CA mutation frequency, in biopsy site, or in prior treatment lines, indicating that it is not simply a more heavily pretreated subset. Its association with shorter time to subsequent progression persisted after adjustment for line of therapy and visceral involvement, with an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.81 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.19 to 2.75.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
Our data separate two classes of alteration in endocrine resistance: those present from the outset, such as PIK3CA mutation, and those selected by therapy, such as ESR1 mutation and RB1 loss. Plasma-based work has shown that ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations detectable before starting an aromatase inhibitor are associated with markedly shorter progression-free survival on that agent, which is consistent with the exposure-dependent enrichment we observe in aromatase inhibitor-treated metastases. Separately, functional profiling across estrogen receptor-positive cell lines has shown that E2F transcriptional output, rather than RB1 mutation status alone, tracks with insensitivity to CDK4/6 inhibition; our finding of an RB1-intact, E2F-high subgroup with rapid progression suggests that this transcriptional axis identifies a clinically distinct population.

The practical consequence concerns which specimen should be tested and when. An archival primary tumor will recover the early, clonal alterations and will systematically miss the selected ones, which are the alterations that bear on the next treatment decision. Our observation that no matched primary carried a ligand-binding domain substitution, while one in five metastases did, quantifies the size of that gap for a single gene. Because the gap is created by treatment rather than by time, it will widen as first-line regimens become more effective and the interval between primary surgery and metastatic decision-making lengthens.

Several limitations qualify these conclusions. Matched primaries were available for fewer than half of participants, and their availability was not random: patients treated at our institution from the outset were overrepresented, which may bias the clonal analyses toward tumors managed in an academic setting. Detection of a subclonal variant in the primary depends on both tumor content and sequencing depth, so our inference that most metastatic alterations descend from minor pre-existing populations rests on modeling rather than direct observation and should be regarded as a statement about the most parsimonious history rather than proof of it. Biopsy site distribution reflects accessibility, and bone lesions in particular are underrepresented relative to their clinical frequency.

Finally, the size of the group with no recovered driver deserves emphasis. Roughly half of the specimens carried no alteration that plausibly explained endocrine resistance, and within that group the transcriptional data identified a phenotype associated with rapid subsequent progression. This suggests that continuing to enlarge sequencing panels is unlikely to close the explanatory gap, and that the more productive direction is to characterize transcriptional and regulatory states in the same specimens. Whether those states are heritable properties of subclones or reversible responses to treatment is not answerable from bulk data and will require single-cell resolution.

title: ESR1 Ligand-Binding Domain Mutations in Plasma Circulating Tumor DNA Predict Inferior Outcome on Aromatase Inhibitor Therapy

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
We measured ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations in pretreatment plasma from 486 patients with hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer starting an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant. Droplet digital PCR assays covering Y537S, Y537N, Y537C, D538G, E380Q, and L536P detected at least one mutation in 28.6 percent of patients previously exposed to an aromatase inhibitor and in 2.1 percent of endocrine-naive patients. Among patients starting a further aromatase inhibitor, median progression-free survival was 3.9 months for mutation-positive versus 8.4 months for mutation-negative disease, with a hazard ratio of 2.12 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.61 to 2.79. No such difference was seen among patients starting fulvestrant. Multiple distinct ligand-binding domain substitutions coexisted in 38 percent of mutation-positive samples, indicating that endocrine resistance arises independently in several tumor populations within the same patient.

Participants were enrolled at eleven centers between 2013 and 2016 and were sampled before the first dose of the study line of therapy, so that the measurement corresponds to the moment at which the treatment decision was made. Median age was 61 years, 68.3 percent had visceral involvement, and the median number of prior endocrine lines for advanced disease was one. Treatment assignment was made by the treating physician without knowledge of the plasma result, which was released only after the database was locked, so the observed association between mutation status and outcome cannot have been produced by the result influencing the choice of therapy.

The magnitude of the interaction between mutation status and treatment class is the central result. Mutation-positive patients did poorly on a further aromatase inhibitor and comparatively well on fulvestrant, while mutation-negative patients did similarly on both, and the formal interaction test supports this pattern rather than a simple prognostic effect. This is the distinction that determines whether a test should change treatment rather than merely predict outcome, and it is the reason we report the interaction as the primary analytic result rather than the two hazard ratios separately.

Assay performance supports the low prevalence estimate in endocrine-naive patients. Across 60 healthy donor specimens no assay returned a call above the reporting threshold, and contrived dilutions were recovered accurately to 0.05 percent fractional abundance. The ten positive calls among endocrine-naive participants were each confirmed on an independent aliquot, and in seven of them the corresponding substitution was subsequently identified in an archival tumor specimen, indicating that these represent genuine low-frequency events rather than analytic artifact.

sections.name: Introduction
