sections.text:
Estrogen deprivation by aromatase inhibition selects for receptor variants that no longer require ligand. These substitutions cluster in helix 12 of the ligand-binding domain and stabilize the agonist conformation, producing constitutive transcriptional activity. They are essentially absent from untreated primary tumors, so tissue obtained at diagnosis cannot be used to detect them, and metastatic rebiopsy is often impractical. Circulating tumor DNA offers a route to serial measurement, but its clinical value depends on whether detection changes what should be done. Because fulvestrant binds and destabilizes the mutant receptor while aromatase inhibition acts upstream of it, the two classes of agent might be expected to differ in their vulnerability to these mutations, a prediction that has not been tested prospectively at scale.

The mechanistic argument for that prediction is straightforward and worth stating explicitly, because it determines what kind of study can test it. Aromatase inhibition lowers circulating estrogen and thereby reduces occupancy of a receptor that requires ligand; a receptor locked in the agonist conformation is indifferent to how much ligand is available, so lowering it further accomplishes nothing. An agent that binds the receptor directly and promotes its removal acts downstream of that indifference and should retain at least some activity. The prediction is therefore not that mutation-positive patients do badly, but that they do badly on one class specifically.

Testing a prediction of that shape requires a study in which both classes are represented and in which the assignment to class is not influenced by the test result. Most published series have been single-arm or have reported outcomes on mixed regimens, which permits estimation of a prognostic effect but not of an interaction. It also requires that the measurement be made before treatment starts rather than at progression, since a sample drawn at progression describes the population that escaped rather than the one present when the decision was made.

Finally, the number of distinct substitutions present in a single patient has received little attention despite an obvious implication. If several independent populations have each solved the same problem with a different substitution, then the tumor has demonstrated a capacity for parallel escape, and an agent that addresses one substitution will be met by the others. We therefore designed the assay panel to detect six recurrent substitutions independently rather than to report a single binary result, so that the number and the relative abundance of coexisting variants could be described.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text:
Plasma was collected before the first dose of endocrine therapy and processed within 4 hours into 4-mL aliquots. Cell-free DNA was extracted from 4 mL and quantified by fluorometry, with a median yield of 24 nanograms. Each of six droplet digital PCR assays was run in duplicate with 20,000 accepted droplets per well and mutant calls requiring three or more positive droplets and a fractional abundance above 0.05 percent. Assay specificity was established on 60 plasma samples from healthy donors. Progression-free survival was analyzed by Cox regression stratified by line of therapy and adjusted for visceral involvement, prior chemotherapy, and performance status. A prespecified interaction test evaluated whether mutation status modified the effect of aromatase inhibitor versus fulvestrant.

Blood was drawn into cell-stabilizing tubes and centrifuged in two stages, with the second stage at 16,000 g to remove residual cellular material, since incomplete depletion of leukocytes dilutes tumor-derived fragments with genomic DNA and depresses apparent fractional abundance. Extraction used a column-based method with a fixed elution volume, and the entire eluate was carried into the assay so that input was maximized rather than normalized to a fixed mass. Total input in genome equivalents was recorded for every specimen and is reported alongside every negative call, because a negative result from a specimen containing few genome equivalents carries less information than one from a specimen containing many.

Each assay was validated against synthetic templates spanning 0.02 to 5 percent fractional abundance in a wild-type background, run on five separate days by two operators. The limit of blank was established from 60 healthy donor specimens and 24 no-template controls, and the reporting threshold was set above the highest observed background for each assay. Positive calls at fractional abundance below 0.2 percent required confirmation on an independent aliquot. Operators were blinded to clinical characteristics and outcome, and specimen identity was masked by a laboratory accession number.

Progression-free survival was defined from the first dose of the study line of therapy to radiographic progression by RECIST version 1.1 or death from any cause, with imaging performed according to local practice at intervals of 8 to 12 weeks. The prespecified primary analysis was the interaction between mutation status and treatment class in a Cox model containing both main effects, with stratification by line of therapy. Secondary analyses examined outcome by number of distinct substitutions and by total mutant molecules per milliliter, the latter modeled on a log scale. Proportional hazards assumptions were assessed by scaled Schoenfeld residuals, and no violation was detected for the primary model.

sections.name: Results
sections.text:
Mutation prevalence rose with cumulative aromatase inhibitor exposure, from 11.4 percent below 18 months to 41.7 percent above 36 months. D538G was the commonest single substitution at 44 percent of positive samples, followed by Y537S at 27 percent. Median fractional abundance was 1.9 percent with a range from 0.06 to 42 percent. The interaction between mutation status and treatment class was significant, with a p value of 0.004. Among mutation-positive patients, fulvestrant gave a median progression-free survival of 5.7 months against 3.9 months for a further aromatase inhibitor. Patients carrying three or more distinct substitutions had the shortest outcome at 2.8 months, and their disease burden as measured by total mutant molecules per milliliter was fourfold higher at baseline.

Of 486 enrolled patients, 471 provided an evaluable pretreatment specimen; the 15 exclusions were for insufficient volume or for processing outside the 4-hour window. Median cell-free DNA input was 7,200 genome equivalents, and 94.1 percent of specimens exceeded 3,000 genome equivalents, the threshold below which a negative call was flagged as uninformative. Among mutation-negative patients, outcomes on the two treatment classes were similar, with median progression-free survival of 8.4 months on a further aromatase inhibitor and 8.9 months on fulvestrant, which is the comparison that gives the interaction its interpretation.

The relationship between substitution number and outcome was monotonic. Patients with a single substitution had a median progression-free survival of 4.8 months, those with two 3.6 months, and those with three or more 2.8 months, and the trend remained after adjustment for total mutant molecules per milliliter, indicating that the number of distinct populations carries information beyond overall burden. Among patients carrying both Y537S and D538G, the two fractional abundances differed by more than fivefold in 61 percent of cases, so the coexisting variants were rarely at comparable frequency.

Prespecified subgroup analyses showed consistent effects across visceral and non-visceral disease, across performance status categories, and across the first and second lines of therapy for advanced disease. No association was found between mutation status and prior chemotherapy exposure or between mutation status and biopsy-confirmed histologic subtype. Total mutant molecules per milliliter was independently associated with progression-free survival with a hazard ratio of 1.44 per log unit and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.22 to 1.70, so both the presence of a substitution and the amount of disease carrying it contributed to outcome.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
These results support measuring ESR1 status in plasma before each change of endocrine therapy rather than relying on archival tissue. Sequencing of paired primary and metastatic tumors has shown that ligand-binding domain mutations are absent from matched primaries and appear only in treatment-exposed metastases, which explains why archival testing is uninformative here. The coexistence of several substitutions in more than a third of positive samples argues against a single dominant escape route and suggests that agents retaining activity against all common variants will be required. Our finding that fulvestrant benefit is preserved in mutation-positive disease provides a rationale for the next-generation oral antiestrogens now entering trials, several of which were designed specifically against helix 12 variants.

The interaction result should be interpreted with care about what it does and does not establish. It establishes that mutation status modifies the relative performance of the two treatment classes, which is the property required for a test to guide treatment. It does not establish that fulvestrant is adequate therapy for mutation-positive disease: a median of 5.7 months is better than 3.9 but is not a good outcome, and the group carrying three or more substitutions did poorly regardless of what they received. The clinically useful reading is that continuing to lower estrogen in a patient whose receptor no longer requires it is the worst of the available options.

Several limitations apply. Treatment was not randomized, so although the plasma result was withheld until database lock, the choice between classes was made on clinical grounds that may correlate with prognosis in ways our adjustment does not fully capture. The assay panel covers six substitutions and will miss rarer ligand-binding domain events, so our prevalence estimates are lower bounds. Imaging intervals followed local practice rather than a fixed schedule, which introduces interval censoring that is unlikely to differ by mutation status but adds noise. Finally, plasma was drawn at a single time point, so we cannot say whether the substitutions detected were rising, stable, or falling at the moment of measurement.

That last limitation points to the natural extension of this work. A single measurement establishes presence, but the quantity that most plausibly determines behavior is the trajectory, and a substitution present at 0.1 percent and rising may differ clinically from one present at 5 percent and stable. Serial sampling during treatment would allow that distinction to be made and would also indicate whether the divergent frequencies we observe among coexisting substitutions reflect differential selection. We regard the present cross-sectional result as establishing the case for such a study rather than as a complete account.

title: RB1 Alterations and E2F Transcriptional Output Define Intrinsic Insensitivity to CDK4/6 Inhibition in Breast Cancer

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
We profiled 58 estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer lines and 14 patient-derived xenografts for sensitivity to palbociclib and related the results to genotype and transcriptional state. RB1-null models were uniformly insensitive, with half-maximal growth inhibition above 3 micromolar, but RB1 status accounted for only 6 of 21 insensitive models. An eleven-gene E2F output score measured before drug exposure separated sensitive from insensitive models with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.88, outperforming RB1 mutation status, CDKN2A deletion, and cyclin D1 amplification. High E2F output in RB1-intact models was associated with CCNE1 amplification or cyclin E1 protein elevation in 9 of 12 cases, and short hairpin depletion of CCNE1 in those models restored palbociclib sensitivity and restored control of the restriction point.

The panel was assembled to span the genotypes proposed to govern response rather than to represent the frequency with which they occur in patients, so that each candidate explanation would be represented by enough models to be evaluated. Twelve models carried CDKN2A deletion, nine carried cyclin D1 amplification, eight carried CCNE1 amplification, and six carried biallelic RB1 inactivation, with partial overlap among these groups. All models were screened under identical conditions in a single laboratory over a nine-month period, with a common reference line included on every plate to permit correction for drift.

The comparison between genotype-based and transcription-based prediction is the central result and was prespecified. Each candidate genotype was evaluated as a binary classifier against the same sensitivity calls, and the eleven-gene score was evaluated as a continuous one, with performance summarized by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve and compared by the DeLong test. The transcriptional score outperformed every genotype individually and outperformed a combined genotype model, and the difference was concentrated in models with intact RB1, where genotype-based prediction has nothing to offer.

The functional experiments establish that the association is not merely descriptive. Depleting the transcript responsible for the alternative kinase activity in cyclin E1-high, RB1-intact models shifted sensitivity by more than an order of magnitude and restored the phosphorylation pattern seen in sensitive models, indicating that the elevated output is a cause of insensitivity rather than a marker of some other property. The reciprocal experiment in cyclin E1-low models produced no such shift, confirming that the effect is specific to models in which the axis is active.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text:
Palbociclib and its congeners act by preventing CDK4- and CDK6-mediated phosphorylation of RB1, thereby holding E2F transcription factors in an inactive complex and blocking entry into S phase. The obvious corollary is that tumors lacking RB1 cannot respond, and this has been confirmed in several systems. What has been much less clear is whether RB1 status is sufficient to predict response, because in clinical series RB1 loss is present in fewer than 5 percent of tumors while primary insensitivity is far more common. Several groups have proposed that the functional state of the pathway, rather than the mutation status of any single gene, determines the response. Testing this requires a panel large enough to separate transcriptional and genetic explanations.

The arithmetic of the discrepancy is what makes the question pressing. If RB1 loss occurred in 5 percent of tumors and accounted for all primary insensitivity, then insensitivity should be a 5 percent problem; instead a substantial minority of patients derive little benefit from the addition of these agents. The excess must be explained by something else, and the candidates fall into two groups: other genomic lesions in the same pathway, and functional states that do not require any lesion. These have been argued for on theoretical grounds without being compared directly in a system large enough to distinguish them.

Comparing them requires a design that avoids two common problems. First, sensitivity must be assessed under conditions that are identical across models, since apparent differences in half-maximal inhibitory concentration are readily produced by differences in seeding density, assay duration, and doubling time. Second, the predictors must be measured before drug exposure, since a state induced by treatment cannot be used to select patients for it. We addressed both by screening under a fixed protocol with a shared reference line and by profiling untreated cells and untreated xenograft tissue.

The eleven transcripts comprising the output score were selected a priori from known targets of the transcription factors held inactive by an intact pathway, rather than derived from the sensitivity data by feature selection. This choice sacrifices some performance in exchange for interpretability and for the ability to evaluate the score as a hypothesis rather than as a fitted model. It also means that the reported discrimination is not inflated by selection on the same data, which is a recurrent problem with expression-based predictors of drug response.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text:
Cell lines were authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling and screened in ten-point dose response over 6 days with CellTiter-Glo readout, in triplicate on three separate occasions. Xenografts were treated with palbociclib at 90 mg/kg daily by oral gavage for 28 days, with eight mice per arm, and response was defined as a tumor growth inhibition index above 60 percent. RNA sequencing was performed on untreated cells and on untreated xenograft tissue. The E2F output score was computed as the mean z-score of MCM2, MCM6, CCNE2, CDC6, E2F1, RRM2, TYMS, PCNA, CDT1, GINS2, and MYBL2. RB1 phosphorylation at serine 780 and serine 807 was quantified by capillary immunoassay at 0, 6, and 24 hours after drug exposure.

Seeding densities were determined individually for each line so that untreated wells remained in exponential growth throughout the 6-day assay, which prevents slow-growing lines from appearing artifactually insensitive through confluence. Drug was replenished at day 3. Each plate contained a common reference line, and plates on which the reference deviated by more than twofold from its running median half-maximal inhibitory concentration were discarded and repeated. Insensitivity was defined prospectively as a half-maximal growth inhibition above 1 micromolar, a threshold set from the distribution observed in a pilot set of twelve lines before the main screen began.

RNA was extracted from cells harvested in exponential growth at the same passage used for screening, and from xenograft tissue snap-frozen within 3 minutes of resection. Libraries were poly-A selected and sequenced to at least 30 million paired reads, and transcript abundance was quantified with a transcriptome-aware pseudoaligner. The output score was computed within each experiment by z-scoring across models, so that the score is a relative measure within the panel rather than an absolute one; we report the raw transcript abundances alongside the score so that the computation can be reproduced or replaced.

Short hairpin depletion used two independent constructs per target with a non-targeting control, delivered by lentiviral transduction and selected for 5 days before assay, with knockdown verified by transcript and protein measurement in every experiment. Statistical comparisons of classifier performance used the DeLong test for correlated areas under the curve. Xenograft growth data were analyzed by mixed-effects models with model identity as a random effect. All animal procedures were approved by the institutional animal care and use committee, and caliper measurements were made by an operator blinded to treatment arm.

sections.name: Results
sections.text:
Twenty-one of 58 lines were insensitive. Six carried biallelic RB1 inactivation. Of the remaining fifteen, twelve had E2F output scores in the top quartile, and nine of those twelve had CCNE1 amplification or cyclin E1 protein above the panel median. In sensitive models, palbociclib reduced serine 780 phosphorylation by more than 80 percent within 6 hours, while in cyclin E1-high insensitive models serine 807 phosphorylation persisted at 62 percent of baseline despite complete loss of serine 780 signal, indicating continued phosphorylation by a kinase other than CDK4 or CDK6. CCNE1 knockdown reduced serine 807 phosphorylation and shifted the palbociclib half-maximal inhibitory concentration from 2.8 micromolar to 0.21 micromolar across five models.

Classifier performance differed substantially among the candidate predictors. RB1 status gave an area under the curve of 0.64, CDKN2A deletion 0.55, and cyclin D1 amplification 0.58, none of which differed significantly from chance in this panel. The eleven-gene score gave 0.88, and the difference against RB1 status was significant at p below 0.001 by the DeLong test. A model combining all three genotypes gave 0.69 and did not improve on the transcriptional score when added to it, indicating that the genotypes carry little information beyond what the output score already captures.

The xenograft results reproduced the cell line findings in an intact tissue context. Of 14 xenografts, 5 were insensitive by the growth inhibition criterion, and the output score measured in untreated tumor tissue separated sensitive from insensitive models with the same ordering, with the two lowest-scoring insensitive models both carrying RB1 alterations. Among the three RB1-intact insensitive xenografts, two carried CCNE1 amplification and the third had cyclin E1 protein in the top quintile of the panel without a copy-number change, illustrating that protein elevation occurs without amplification.

The knockdown experiments were performed in five cyclin E1-high, RB1-intact models with two independent hairpins each. Both hairpins produced concordant shifts in every model, and the magnitude of the sensitivity shift correlated with the extent of protein depletion across constructs. In three cyclin E1-low control models, the same constructs produced no meaningful change in half-maximal inhibitory concentration, with shifts below 1.4-fold. Restoration of serine 807 control was accompanied by loss of chromatin-associated replication licensing signal, consistent with reinstated control at the restriction point rather than with a general growth defect.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
Resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition is not a binary consequence of RB1 loss. Our data indicate that a transcriptional readout of pathway activity captures a larger and clinically more relevant population, and that within the RB1-intact insensitive group cyclin E1 is the dominant explanation. This has two implications. First, assays used to select patients should measure pathway output rather than single-gene status. Second, the cyclin E1-high group remains addressable because RB1 protein is present, so agents that block the alternative kinase should restore control. Sequencing of metastatic biopsies has independently described an RB1-intact subgroup with elevated E2F and MYC target expression and rapid progression, which we believe corresponds to the population defined functionally here.

The phosphosite data provide the mechanistic account that makes the transcriptional observation interpretable. Complete loss of signal at one residue with persistence at another during full drug exposure is difficult to explain except by a second kinase acting on the same substrate, and the restoration of control by depleting the relevant cyclin identifies which one. This also explains why single-gene genotype performs poorly as a predictor: the relevant quantity is the total kinase activity converging on the substrate, and no single gene reports it.

The limitations of a model panel study should be stated plainly. Cell lines have been propagated for decades under selection for growth in culture and are enriched for alterations that confer that property, so the frequency of any genotype in our panel says nothing about its frequency in patients; we selected models to represent genotypes rather than to represent a population. The xenografts are fewer and were assessed with a categorical response criterion that compresses a continuous outcome. And the output score is a relative measure within a panel, so translating it into a threshold applicable to a clinical specimen will require calibration against an external reference rather than direct transfer.

Two directions follow. The first is to determine whether the score, or a calibrated version of it, predicts outcome in patients receiving these agents, which requires pretreatment specimens with linked outcome rather than models. The second is to test whether pharmacologic blockade of the alternative kinase restores sensitivity as genetic depletion does, which is the experiment that would convert this from an explanation into a treatment strategy. Selective agents against that kinase are in development, and the models characterized here provide a defined system in which to evaluate them.

title: Acquired RB1 Loss and CCNE1 Amplification in Serial Circulating Tumor DNA from Patients Progressing on Palbociclib plus Fulvestrant

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
We analyzed 1,020 plasma samples collected every 8 weeks from 195 patients receiving palbociclib with fulvestrant for hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, using a 74-gene tumor-informed panel with a limit of detection of 0.1 percent variant allele fraction. Alterations detectable at progression but absent at baseline included RB1 truncating or biallelic events in 5.6 percent of patients, CCNE1 copy gain in 16.4 percent, PIK3CA H1047R or E545K in 11.8 percent, and ESR1 ligand-binding domain substitutions in 33.8 percent. Circulating tumor DNA burden began to rise a median of 9.6 weeks before radiographic progression, with an interquartile range of 5.1 to 16.2 weeks. Clonal evolution modeling showed that acquired RB1 events arose in populations that also carried the dominant baseline truncal alterations, indicating direct descent rather than the outgrowth of an unrelated lineage.

The cohort was drawn from a single institutional registry with a fixed sampling schedule, which is what makes the timing analysis possible. Median age was 60 years, 62 percent had visceral involvement, and treatment was first-line for advanced disease in 44 percent and second-line in the remainder. Sampling adherence was high, with 89 percent of scheduled draws obtained within a 2-week window, and the median number of specimens per patient was five with a maximum of fourteen. Patients contributed samples until radiographic progression, after which a final draw was obtained within 4 weeks in 81 percent.

Two categories of result follow from this design. The first concerns what is acquired: which alterations appear during treatment in patients whose baseline plasma was adequately sampled and negative at the relevant locus. The second concerns when: how far in advance of the imaging change the molecular signal becomes apparent, and whether that interval differs by alteration class. Because both depend on baseline negativity being established rather than assumed, we report the number of informative molecules at each locus alongside every claim of acquisition.

A third finding concerns early response. Patients whose tumor DNA became undetectable by the week 8 draw had markedly longer progression-free survival than those in whom it did not, a difference larger than that associated with any acquired alteration. This suggests that the depth of the initial molecular response carries more prognostic weight than the identity of the lesion that eventually emerges, and it identifies an early time point at which a poor trajectory is already apparent.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text:
Combination of an aromatase inhibitor or fulvestrant with a CDK4/6 inhibitor is now standard first- and second-line therapy in hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer, yet resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition is essentially universal. Progression biopsies are obtained in a minority of patients, and the alterations reported from such series may not represent the population. Serial plasma sampling offers an alternative that is both repeatable and unbiased with respect to lesion accessibility, and it adds a temporal dimension that tissue cannot: the interval between the appearance of an alteration and the appearance of a radiographic change. We applied dense plasma sampling to a uniformly treated cohort in order to establish which alterations are selected during treatment and when they first become detectable.

The accessibility bias in tissue-based progression series is easy to state and hard to correct. Patients biopsied at progression are those with a lesion that a radiologist is willing to sample, which favors liver and soft tissue over bone and favors larger lesions over smaller ones. If the biology of escape differs by site, and there is reason to think it might, then the resulting frequency estimates describe a subset rather than the population. Plasma is not free of bias, since shedding differs by site and by burden, but its biases are different and can be characterized by measuring total burden alongside each alteration.

The temporal question cannot be addressed by tissue at all. A progression biopsy establishes that an alteration is present at progression; it cannot establish when it became present, and inferring timing from a single specimen requires assumptions about growth rates that are rarely justified. A series of specimens collected at fixed intervals from before the first dose converts each patient into a trajectory, from which the moment of inflection can be estimated and compared against the date on which imaging changed.

We chose an 8-week sampling interval to match the imaging schedule in routine use, so that the comparison between molecular and radiographic change would be made on comparable footing and so that the resulting estimate of lead time would describe what a clinician could actually have observed. A tumor-informed panel was used rather than a fixed hotspot panel so that copy-number changes and patient-specific variants could be followed alongside recurrent substitutions.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text:
Patients enrolled on an institutional registry beginning palbociclib 125 mg daily on a three-weeks-on one-week-off schedule with fulvestrant 500 mg. Plasma was drawn at baseline and every 8 weeks until progression. Hybrid-capture libraries were sequenced to 20,000-fold raw and 3,000-fold deduplicated depth with unique molecular identifiers. Copy gain was called using a normalized coverage ratio with a threshold of 1.6 relative to a panel of 96 normal plasma controls. Baseline absence was defined as zero supporting molecules in a sample with at least 8,000 informative molecules at that locus. Clonal reconstruction used cancer cell fraction estimates corrected for tumor content inferred from truncal variants. Lead time was estimated by fitting piecewise-linear splines to log-transformed tumor DNA burden and comparing the fitted change point with the RECIST progression date.

Blood was collected into cell-stabilizing tubes and processed within 6 hours, and the full cell-free DNA eluate was carried into library preparation. Unique molecular identifiers were incorporated during adapter ligation, and consensus reads were formed from families of at least two members, with singletons retained separately for the purpose of estimating input molecules but excluded from variant calling. Matched leukocyte DNA was sequenced on the same panel for every patient, and variants present in that material were removed before analysis, which is essential in a population where clonal hematopoietic variants in genes such as TP53 and PPM1D are common and would otherwise be misread as tumor-derived.

Radiographic assessment was performed every 8 to 12 weeks according to registry protocol and was read by the treating radiologist, with all progression events subsequently confirmed by a central reviewer blinded to plasma results. Laboratory staff had no access to imaging dates or clinical outcomes, and the plasma analysis was locked before the two datasets were joined. Total tumor DNA burden was summarized as the mean variant allele fraction of truncal variants weighted by their informative molecule counts, which is more stable across time points than the maximum fraction.

Statistical analysis treated acquisition and timing separately. Acquisition frequencies are reported as proportions with exact binomial confidence intervals, with the denominator restricted to patients meeting the informative-molecule threshold at the relevant locus. Associations between acquired alterations and time to progression were tested by Cox regression with the alteration entered as a time-dependent covariate to avoid immortal time bias. Change points were estimated per patient from piecewise-linear spline fits, and lead time is summarized as a median with interquartile range. Patients with fewer than three positive time points did not contribute to the timing analysis, and their number is reported.

sections.name: Results
sections.text:
Median follow-up was 26 months and 168 patients progressed. Baseline circulating tumor DNA was detectable in 88.2 percent. Eleven patients acquired RB1 events, of whom nine had no detectable RB1 alteration in more than 12,000 informative molecules at baseline. Acquired CCNE1 gain was associated with a shorter time to progression, at 7.1 versus 13.4 months, with a hazard ratio of 1.87 and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.24 to 2.82. PIK3CA H1047R emerged in 23 patients, of whom 14 had wild-type baseline plasma. Patients in whom tumor DNA burden fell below the limit of detection by week 8 had a median progression-free survival of 21.3 months against 8.9 months for those in whom it did not, with a p value below 0.001.

Of the 1,020 specimens analyzed, 987 met quality thresholds, and the median number of informative molecules per locus was 14,600. The 23 patients with undetectable baseline tumor DNA had a longer median progression-free survival than the cohort as a whole, at 24.8 months, and none of them acquired an RB1 event, though the small number limits inference. Among the 168 progression events, 142 patients had at least three positive time points and contributed to the timing analysis; the 26 excluded had lower baseline burden and shorter follow-up.

Lead time differed modestly by alteration class. The rise in total burden preceded imaging by a median of 9.6 weeks overall, and the first appearance of an ESR1 substitution preceded imaging by a median of 12.1 weeks, while acquired CCNE1 gain was detected a median of 6.4 weeks before imaging, consistent with copy-number calls requiring higher burden to be made confidently. Acquired RB1 events were detected a median of 8.8 weeks before imaging in the nine patients with adequate baseline coverage. In 19 patients the fitted change point fell after the imaging date, so the signal did not always precede the scan.

Coexistence of acquired alterations was common. Thirty-one patients acquired two or more of the four prespecified alteration classes, most frequently an ESR1 substitution together with a CCNE1 gain, and these patients had the shortest time to progression at a median of 6.2 months. Among patients acquiring ESR1 substitutions, 41 percent acquired more than one distinct substitution during follow-up, and in 12 patients a substitution that was dominant at one time point was overtaken by another at a later one. Clonal reconstruction assigned acquired RB1 events to lineages carrying the dominant truncal variants in 10 of 11 cases.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
Our findings extend earlier functional work showing that RB1-null models are uniformly insensitive to palbociclib and that an E2F transcriptional output score identifies a larger RB1-intact insensitive population in which cyclin E1 is elevated. We show that the same two lesions, RB1 inactivation and CCNE1 gain, can be acquired under treatment pressure in patients and can be detected in plasma before imaging changes. The clinical implication is that a plasma test performed at 8-week intervals identifies a substantial fraction of patients months before conventional progression, which creates a window in which a change of therapy could be made against a smaller tumor burden. Whether acting in that window improves outcome requires randomized testing.

The relative frequencies of the two lesions deserve emphasis because they bear on where effort should be directed. Acquired RB1 events occurred in fewer than 6 percent of patients while CCNE1 gain occurred in roughly one in six, so the population in which the pathway remains addressable is substantially larger than the population in which it does not. That asymmetry argues for developing agents against the alternative kinase activity rather than concentrating on the smaller group whose downstream brake has been removed, for whom no upstream intervention can help.

Several limitations qualify the timing results. Change points estimated from five or six observations carry substantial uncertainty, and our interquartile range of 5.1 to 16.2 weeks reflects genuine biological variation combined with that estimation error in proportions we cannot separate. Nineteen patients had fitted change points falling after the imaging date, which may reflect low-shedding disease, sampling gaps, or model misfit. The sampling interval also bounds the resolution: a lead time cannot be estimated more finely than the interval between draws, so our median should be read as an approximation rather than a precise figure.

Two further caveats concern generalizability. The cohort was treated at a single institution with an unusually high sampling adherence rate, and lead times in routine practice with less complete sampling would be shorter. And detection depends on shedding, so patients with bone-predominant disease, who are underrepresented among those with detectable baseline tumor DNA, are also those for whom the approach is least informative. Any prospective evaluation of an early-switching strategy will need to account for the fact that the patients most likely to benefit from earlier information are not uniformly those from whom it can be obtained.

title: Cyclin E1-CDK2 Activation Confers Palbociclib Resistance and Is Targetable with a Selective CDK2 Inhibitor in Patient-Derived Models

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
Elevated cyclin E1 is the commonest correlate of resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition in RB1-intact breast cancer, but whether it is causal and whether it is druggable have not been established in patient-derived systems. We show that enforced cyclin E1 expression in MCF7 and T47D shifts the palbociclib half-maximal inhibitory concentration by 18-fold and 12-fold respectively, and that low-molecular-weight cyclin E1 isoforms produce a larger shift than full-length protein. The selective CDK2 inhibitor PF-07104091 restored control of the cell cycle in these models and in six patient-derived xenografts with high cyclin E1, producing tumor growth inhibition of 71 percent as a single agent and 89 percent combined with palbociclib. Sequential rather than concurrent dosing preserved efficacy while halving the neutrophil nadir, an outcome that has direct implications for how these agents should be combined in preclinical models and in patients.

The study was designed around the distinction between correlation and dependence, which the existing literature has not resolved. Correlative data establish that models with more of this protein respond less; they do not establish that removing the resulting kinase activity restores response, nor that the relationship holds in tumors carrying the alteration as it arises in patients rather than as it is engineered in a laboratory line. We therefore paired enforced expression in two well-characterized lines with pharmacologic intervention in fourteen patient-derived xenografts, six of them from patients with documented clinical progression on palbociclib.

The isoform result was not anticipated at the outset and has practical consequences. Enforced expression of the truncated species produced both a larger sensitivity shift and more persistent substrate phosphorylation than the full-length protein at matched total protein abundance, which means that two tumors with identical total protein can differ in dependence according to how that protein is distributed between species. Since the immunohistochemical assays in routine use do not distinguish them, this is a measurable property that current practice discards.

The schedule finding is the most immediately translatable. Concurrent exposure produced the greatest tumor effect and the greatest marrow suppression, and alternating weekly blocks recovered most of the tumor effect at roughly half the hematologic cost. Because marrow tolerance is the constraint that will determine whether these two classes can be given together at all, a schedule that preserves efficacy while relieving that constraint is worth establishing before combination trials are designed.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text:
Serial plasma sequencing in patients progressing on palbociclib with fulvestrant showed that CCNE1 copy gain emerges during treatment in roughly one in six patients and is associated with a shorter time to progression, while acquired RB1 events occur in fewer than 6 percent. That distribution implies that the cyclin E1 axis is the larger of the two addressable problems, since RB1 loss removes the substrate on which any upstream agent depends whereas cyclin E1 elevation leaves the pathway intact and merely bypasses the drug target. CDK2 is the obligate partner of cyclin E1 and is now the subject of several selective inhibitor programs. Here we test causality and therapeutic tractability across cell lines, organoids, and patient-derived xenografts, including models established from patients with documented clinical progression on palbociclib.

The causality question has been difficult to settle because the usual experimental approach introduces its own artifact. Enforced expression from a strong constitutive promoter produces protein at concentrations far above anything observed in tumors, and at those concentrations the endogenous inhibitors of the kinase are titrated out, so the resulting insensitivity may reflect the overexpression rather than the biology. We addressed this by using an inducible cassette titrated to produce protein within twofold of the concentrations measured in amplified tumors, verified against recombinant standards.

The isoform question compounds the difficulty. Proteolytic cleavage generates species that lack the surface through which the endogenous inhibitors bind, so a given quantity of truncated protein is expected to produce more kinase activity than the same quantity of full-length protein. If the two species differ in this way, then a measurement that sums them will predict dependence imperfectly, and the failure will be systematic rather than random. Testing this requires expressing each species separately and measuring both substrate phosphorylation and growth.

Finally, the therapeutic question requires models that reflect the clinical situation in which the agents would be used. A cyclin E1-high line that has never seen a CDK4/6 inhibitor is a test of the mechanism; a xenograft established from a patient whose disease progressed on palbociclib is a test of the treatment. We included both, and we treated marrow reserve as a co-primary consideration rather than as a safety footnote, because two agents acting on the same proliferative machinery will compete for the same tolerance.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text:
Full-length CCNE1 and the elastase-generated low-molecular-weight isoforms T1 and T2 were expressed from a doxycycline-inducible cassette at levels within twofold of those seen in CCNE1-amplified tumors, verified by capillary immunoassay against recombinant standards. Fourteen patient-derived xenografts were characterized for cyclin E1 protein and CCNE1 copy number. Preclinical models were treated with palbociclib at 90 mg/kg daily, PF-07104091 at 30 mg/kg twice daily, or combinations given concurrently or in 7-day alternating blocks, with eight mice per arm. RB1 phosphosite occupancy was measured by parallel reaction monitoring. DNA replication licensing was assessed by chromatin-bound MCM2. Neutrophil counts were obtained weekly. Growth data were analyzed with mixed-effects models treating xenograft identity as a random effect.

Induction was titrated by doxycycline concentration in a preliminary experiment, and the concentration producing protein within the target range was fixed for all subsequent work; protein abundance was verified in every experiment rather than assumed from the induction condition. Cells were assayed 48 hours after induction so that the phenotype reflected established rather than acute expression. Parental lines carrying the empty cassette and induced with the same doxycycline concentration served as controls throughout, which excludes effects of doxycycline itself on proliferation.

Xenografts were propagated in NSG mice at passages 3 to 6 and authenticated by short tandem repeat profiling against the originating patient specimen where available. Cyclin E1 protein was measured on untreated tumor harvested at a standardized volume, with three independent tumors per model, and CCNE1 copy number was determined from targeted sequencing of the same material. Drug exposure was confirmed by terminal plasma concentration in satellite animals for each agent and schedule, which excludes the possibility that a schedule difference reflects a difference in achieved exposure rather than in timing.

Neutrophil counts were obtained weekly from the same animals contributing tumor measurements, using submandibular sampling with a fixed volume limit, so that efficacy and marrow effects are paired within animal. Tumor volumes were measured by an operator blinded to arm, and animals were randomized to arm by cage after stratification on starting volume. Growth data were log-transformed and analyzed in a mixed-effects framework with xenograft identity as a random effect and arm as a fixed effect; growth inhibition is reported relative to vehicle at the last time point at which all arms remained on study.

sections.name: Results
sections.text:
Induction of low-molecular-weight cyclin E1 sustained serine 807 phosphorylation of RB1 at 74 percent of baseline during palbociclib exposure and maintained MCM2 chromatin loading, whereas full-length cyclin E1 sustained it at 48 percent. PF-07104091 reduced serine 807 phosphorylation to 12 percent and produced G1 accumulation in both settings. Across six cyclin E1-high xenografts, single-agent CDK2 inhibition gave 71 percent tumor growth inhibition and the concurrent combination gave 89 percent, but concurrent dosing reduced the neutrophil nadir to 0.6 times ten to the ninth per liter. Alternating 7-day blocks achieved 84 percent inhibition with a nadir of 1.4. In three cyclin E1-low xenografts, CDK2 inhibition produced 19 percent inhibition, confirming dependence on the axis.

In the enforced expression experiments, the sensitivity shift tracked the isoform. Full-length protein shifted the half-maximal inhibitory concentration by 18-fold in MCF7 and 12-fold in T47D; the truncated species shifted it by 34-fold and 26-fold respectively at matched total protein abundance. Cell cycle analysis showed that the difference lay in the fraction of cells escaping G1 arrest during palbociclib exposure, at 31 percent for the truncated species against 14 percent for full length, with untreated controls at 58 percent. Withdrawal of induction reversed the shift within 72 hours in both lines.

Among the fourteen characterized xenografts, cyclin E1 protein and CCNE1 copy number were only moderately correlated, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.61, and three models with copy number in the normal range had protein in the top quintile. Protein abundance predicted palbociclib growth inhibition better than copy number, and the truncated fraction added information beyond total protein in a model containing both. Of the six models from patients with documented progression on palbociclib, five had cyclin E1 protein above the panel median.

Schedule effects were consistent across models. Concurrent dosing produced the greatest tumor growth inhibition in five of six cyclin E1-high models and the lowest neutrophil nadir in all six. Alternating blocks produced inhibition within 6 percentage points of concurrent dosing in four of six models while approximately doubling the nadir. Weight loss exceeding 10 percent occurred in 4 of 48 animals on concurrent dosing and in none on the alternating schedule. Two animals on concurrent dosing were removed for protocol-defined toxicity criteria and are included in the analysis by their last observation.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
These data establish cyclin E1 as a causal driver rather than a passenger correlate of palbociclib resistance and identify low-molecular-weight isoforms as the more potent form, which matters because standard immunohistochemistry does not resolve them. The efficacy of sequential dosing is the most immediately actionable finding: marrow suppression is the principal barrier to combining two cell cycle-directed agents, and alternating blocks preserved most of the benefit at half the hematologic cost. Functional profiling across estrogen receptor-positive lines previously showed that an E2F output score identifies insensitive models better than RB1 status, and our results suggest that within that group cyclin E1 protein, resolved by isoform, is the assay that should guide assignment to CDK2 inhibition.

The discordance between copy number and protein is worth stating as a practical conclusion in its own right. Selection strategies built on amplification calls will exclude tumors with high protein and no copy-number change, which in our panel comprised three of fourteen models, and will include tumors with amplification and unremarkable protein. Since the alteration is being used to assign patients to a drug whose dose is limited by marrow toxicity, both errors carry real cost, and the correction requires only a protein assay capable of resolving the species.

Limitations of the study concern the models and the schedule. Enforced expression, even at titrated concentrations, is not identical to the endogenous elevation that occurs in tumors, and although the xenograft experiments do not depend on it, the isoform comparison does. Six models is a small number from which to conclude that a schedule generalizes, and the schedule that is optimal in mice will not transfer numerically to humans, whose marrow recovery kinetics and drug half-lives differ. We have therefore expressed the schedule result as a relative trade-off rather than as a recommended interval.

The natural extension is a clinical evaluation in which patients are selected by isoform-resolved protein and assigned to an alternating rather than concurrent schedule. The selection assay would need calibration against a reference standard, and the schedule would need to be derived from human pharmacokinetics rather than transposed from the mouse. Our data provide the mechanistic rationale and the model system for both, and they indicate specifically which patients are unlikely to benefit: those in whom the downstream substrate is absent, where no intervention upstream of it can restore control.

title: Serial Circulating Tumor DNA Allele Fractions of ESR1 Mutations Define Early Molecular Progression During Fulvestrant

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text:
We collected plasma every 4 weeks from 224 patients receiving fulvestrant for hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer and tracked eight ESR1 ligand-binding domain substitutions by droplet digital PCR, with confirmatory 61-gene sequencing at every third time point. A confirmed twofold or greater rise in mutant allele fraction on two consecutive draws preceded radiographic progression by a median of 11.4 weeks, with an interquartile range of 6.0 to 18.7. Sensitivity for subsequent progression within 6 months was 78 percent and specificity was 84 percent. Clonal dynamics differed by substitution: Y537S rose steadily during treatment and dominated at progression in 61 percent of patients carrying it, whereas D538G allele fractions fell in 44 percent of patients even as total tumor DNA increased, indicating that the two variants are under different selective pressure during fulvestrant exposure.

The design was built around the requirement that the molecular criterion be defined before it was evaluated. Molecular progression was specified in the protocol as a confirmed twofold rise above the on-treatment nadir on two consecutive draws separated by at least 4 weeks, and imaging was read centrally by reviewers blinded to the plasma results. This ordering matters because a threshold chosen after inspection of the data will always appear to perform well, and the performance figures reported for such thresholds do not transfer to new patients.

The cohort was sampled more densely than is usual in this setting. Median follow-up was 19 months, the median number of specimens per patient was eleven, and 84 percent of scheduled draws were obtained within a 1-week window. This density is what permits the divergent behavior of individual substitutions to be observed, since a variant that falls while total burden rises will appear simply as a lower fraction in a cross-sectional sample and can only be recognized as falling when its own trajectory is followed.

Two distinct results follow. The first is operational: a defined and confirmable plasma criterion identifies escape roughly three months before imaging does, with a false-positive proportion low enough that acting on it would not expose many patients to an unnecessary change of therapy. The second is biological: the substitutions do not behave as a single entity during treatment, which bears on what should be given when the criterion fires.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text:
Treatment decisions in advanced hormone receptor-positive breast cancer are triggered by imaging performed every 8 to 12 weeks, so a change of therapy always follows the underlying escape by an unknown interval. Plasma measurement of tumor DNA could shorten that interval, but only if the signal is specific enough to act on. Earlier work established that ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations measured in pretreatment plasma predict inferior progression-free survival on a further aromatase inhibitor while fulvestrant benefit is preserved, and that several distinct substitutions frequently coexist in the same patient. Those observations were cross-sectional. Whether the trajectory of individual substitutions during treatment carries additional information, and whether a defined rise can serve as an early trigger, has not been established.

The specificity requirement is what distinguishes a monitoring application from a prognostic one. A marker that identifies patients destined to do badly is useful for stratification even if it is imprecise; a marker used to change treatment must be right about the individual, because acting on a false signal exposes a patient who is still benefiting to an unnecessary switch. This asymmetry argues for a criterion built on confirmation across consecutive draws rather than on a single measurement, and for reporting the false-positive proportion among the population in which the criterion would be applied.

The biological question is separable and has received less attention. Ligand-binding domain substitutions differ in the degree to which they stabilize the agonist conformation and in their measured responsiveness to receptor-directed agents, so there is no reason to expect them to behave identically under the same selective pressure. If they do not, then the composition of the mutant population will change during treatment, and the variant that dominates at escape may not be the one that was dominant at the start.

Answering both questions requires dense, protocol-driven sampling with a prespecified criterion, central blinded imaging, and assays capable of tracking individual substitutions rather than reporting an aggregate. We designed the present study to meet those requirements, sampling every 4 weeks rather than at the 8 to 12 week interval used for imaging so that a change occurring between scans could be observed rather than inferred.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text:
Eligible patients were starting fulvestrant 500 mg with or without a CDK4/6 inhibitor. Plasma was drawn at baseline, day 15, and every 4 weeks thereafter. Droplet digital PCR assays covered Y537S, Y537N, Y537C, D538G, E380Q, L536P, L536H, and S463P, each run in duplicate with 20,000 accepted droplets. Molecular progression was prespecified as two consecutive draws showing at least a twofold increase in mutant allele fraction above the on-treatment nadir, with the second draw at least 4 weeks after the first. Imaging was performed every 8 weeks and read centrally, blinded to plasma results. Lead time was estimated by interval-censored methods. Clonal composition was reconstructed at each time point from copy-number-corrected fractions using the 61-gene panel.

Specimens were processed within 4 hours into aliquots, and the full eluate from a 4-mL aliquot was carried into each assay so that input was maximized. Total cell-free DNA and total genome equivalents were recorded for every draw, and mutant allele fraction was reported alongside absolute mutant molecules per milliliter, since a rise in fraction can arise from a fall in the wild-type background as well as from an increase in mutant molecules. The prespecified criterion was applied to fraction, with the absolute measure reported as a sensitivity analysis; the two agreed in 92 percent of criterion events.

Assay validation followed the same procedure for all eight substitutions, using synthetic templates in a wild-type background across 0.02 to 5 percent, replicated on five days by two operators, with limits of blank established from 60 healthy donor specimens and 24 no-template controls. Calls below 0.2 percent required confirmation on an independent aliquot. Laboratory staff were blinded to clinical status and to imaging, and results were not released to treating physicians at any point during the study, so no plasma result could have influenced the timing of a scan or a treatment change.

Sensitivity and specificity for subsequent progression within 6 months were computed among mutation-positive patients, since the criterion is undefined in patients with no detectable substitution. Lead time was estimated by interval-censored methods that place the true onset between the last draw not meeting the criterion and the first draw meeting it, which avoids the systematic understatement produced by using the date of the confirming draw. Comparisons of substitution trajectories used mixed-effects models on log-transformed fractions with patient as a random effect.

sections.name: Results
sections.text:
At least one ESR1 substitution was detected in 96 patients, 42.9 percent of the cohort. Molecular progression was observed in 71 of these, and 64 subsequently progressed radiographically. Seven met the molecular criterion without progressing within 6 months, giving a false-positive proportion of 9.9 percent among mutation-positive patients. Median lead time was 11.4 weeks. Among patients carrying both Y537S and D538G, the Y537S fraction exceeded the D538G fraction at progression in 68 percent of cases, reversing the baseline ordering in 31 percent. Total tumor DNA burden at week 4 was independently associated with progression-free survival with a hazard ratio of 1.62 per log unit and a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.28 to 2.05.

Of 224 enrolled patients, 219 contributed at least three evaluable draws and are included in the analyses. A total of 2,410 specimens were analyzed, with a median of eleven per patient. Among the 96 mutation-positive patients, 38 carried a single substitution, 34 carried two, and 24 carried three or more, and the number carried at baseline did not change in 71 percent of patients during follow-up; in the remainder, a substitution not detectable at baseline appeared during treatment, most commonly Y537S.

The divergent trajectories of the two commonest substitutions were consistent across the cohort. Y537S fractions rose in 74 percent of patients carrying that variant, with a median fitted doubling time of 34 days among those in whom it rose. D538G fractions fell in 44 percent of carriers even as total tumor DNA increased, and in those patients the absolute mutant molecule count for D538G also fell, so the pattern was not an artifact of normalization to a rising background. Mixed-effects modeling confirmed a significant difference in the mean trajectory slope between the two substitutions.

Performance of the criterion was stable across prespecified subgroups. Sensitivity was 78 percent overall, 81 percent among patients receiving fulvestrant with a CDK4/6 inhibitor and 74 percent among those receiving fulvestrant alone; specificity was 84 percent and 83 percent respectively. Among the seven patients meeting the criterion without progressing within 6 months, five progressed between 6 and 11 months, so most were early rather than false in an absolute sense. No patient met the criterion at the baseline or day 15 draws by construction, since the nadir is defined on treatment.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text:
A defined, confirmed rise in mutant allele fraction identifies escape roughly three months before imaging does, and does so with a false-positive proportion low enough to justify testing an intervention. The divergent behavior of Y537S and D538G is the more biologically interesting result. Y537S stabilizes the agonist conformation most strongly and is the least responsive to fulvestrant in reporter systems, so its progressive dominance during fulvestrant exposure is consistent with direct selection. This has implications for agent choice at the time of molecular progression, since a treatment that is equally weak against the emerging population would waste the lead time that the assay provides. A randomized test of early switching is now underway.

The performance figures should be read with attention to the population in which they were computed. Sensitivity and specificity are reported among mutation-positive patients, because the criterion cannot be applied to a patient with no detectable substitution, and mutation-positive patients comprised 43 percent of the cohort. The criterion therefore addresses escape in a defined subset rather than in the whole population, and a monitoring strategy built on it would need a complementary approach for the majority who never develop a detectable ligand-binding domain event.

Limitations include the observational design and the resolution imposed by sampling. Because results were withheld, no treatment change was made on the basis of a molecular event, which preserves the validity of the lead-time estimate but also means that the clinical value of acting on it remains untested. Lead time cannot be resolved more finely than the 4-week sampling interval, and the interval-censored estimate reflects that. Central imaging at 8-week intervals similarly bounds the precision of the comparison, and the true interval between biological and radiographic escape is likely somewhat longer than we report.

The result that a substitution can fall while total burden rises has an implication for study design that we did not anticipate. Any monitoring scheme that reports an aggregate mutant fraction will average across populations moving in opposite directions and will therefore understate the dynamics of both. Tracking substitutions individually is more laborious and, on this evidence, necessary. It also raises the question of whether the falling population is being controlled by the treatment while the rising one is not, which would suggest that the choice of subsequent therapy should be directed at the variant that is rising rather than at the one that was most abundant when treatment began.

title: Therapy-Induced Senescence Limits the Durability of CDK4/6 Inhibition and Is Reversed by BCL-xL-Directed Senolytics

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text: Palbociclib produces a durable arrest rather than cell death in most estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer models. We show that 58 to 74 percent of arrested cells acquire senescence markers, including senescence-associated beta-galactosidase activity, p21 induction, lysosomal expansion, and an interleukin 6 and CXCL8 secretory program, and that this population persists for at least 60 days of continuous exposure. Single-cell RNA sequencing of 61,000 cells from treated xenografts identified a senescent compartment with elevated BCL2L1 and a small subpopulation retaining proliferative transcriptional features. A CRISPR screen performed in cells arrested for 14 days identified BCL2L1 as the dominant survival dependency. The BCL-xL-selective agent A-1331852 eliminated 82 percent of senescent cells and extended time to tumor regrowth from 34 to 71 days across ten patient-derived xenografts and four organoid lines.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text: Clinical responses to CDK4/6 inhibitors are characteristically shallow and prolonged, and disease frequently reaccelerates within weeks of stopping the drug. Both features suggest a large persistent arrested population rather than tumor cell elimination. Work in patient-derived systems has shown that cyclin E1 elevation allows continued phosphorylation of RB1 at serine 807 and permits passage through the restriction point despite full CDK4 and CDK6 blockade, defining one route by which tumors continue to divide. The complementary question, what happens to the cells that do stop dividing, has received far less attention. If arrested cells persist, secrete inflammatory mediators, and can re-enter proliferation, then eliminating them is a distinct therapeutic objective requiring drugs that act on non-dividing cells.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text: Ten patient-derived xenografts and four organoid lines were exposed to palbociclib at 90 mg/kg daily or 500 nanomolar respectively. Senescence was scored by beta-galactosidase histochemistry at pH 6.0, p21 and p16 immunofluorescence, and an eighteen-transcript secretory signature measured by NanoString on laser-captured regions. Single-cell libraries were prepared from dissociated xenografts at days 0, 14, and 42. A 4,000-guide CRISPR library targeting apoptotic regulators was introduced into cells already arrested for 14 days and maintained at 500-fold representation for 12 doublings of the control population. A-1331852 was dosed at 25 mg/kg on two consecutive days per week beginning at day 21. Regrowth was defined as a doubling of nadir tumor volume.

sections.name: Results
sections.text: Senescent fraction rose from 4 percent at baseline to 58 to 74 percent by day 21 and remained above 50 percent at day 60. RB1 protein was retained in all models, and RB1 phosphorylation at serine 780 was suppressed by more than 85 percent throughout. The CRISPR screen returned BCL2L1 as the strongest dependency with a log fold change of minus 3.2, followed by MCL1 at minus 1.4, while BCL2 scored neutral. Navitoclax and A-1331852 both cleared senescent cells, but A-1331852 spared platelets, with a nadir of 148 versus 46 times ten to the ninth per liter. Combination with continuous palbociclib extended median time to regrowth from 34 days to 71 days, with a p value below 0.001 by mixed-effects Cox regression.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text: The durability of CDK4/6 blockade appears to be governed less by how deeply proliferation is suppressed than by what happens to the cells that have stopped. Our data identify BCL-xL as the survival dependency of that reservoir and show that clearing it substantially delays regrowth without deepening the initial arrest. Platelet sparing is practically important because the platelet dependency of navitoclax has limited its clinical development. The secretory program we observe also raises the possibility that arrested cells actively shape the surrounding microenvironment, a question our design cannot address because the xenograft host lacks an adaptive immune system. Testing this in immunocompetent models is the necessary next step.

title: CDK4/6 Inhibition Enhances Antigen Presentation and Potentiates PD-1 Blockade in Estrogen Receptor-Positive Mammary Tumors

sections.name: Abstract
sections.text: We examined the immune consequences of abemaciclib in three estrogen receptor-positive syngeneic mammary tumor models. Abemaciclib increased surface MHC class I abundance by 3.4-fold within 7 days, derepressed endogenous retroviral transcripts with a corresponding rise in cytosolic double-stranded RNA, and induced type III interferon transcription. Regulatory T cell proliferation was suppressed more than that of CD8-positive effector cells, raising the effector to regulatory ratio from 2.1 to 7.8. Mass cytometry of 1.2 million cells showed expansion of an activated CD8 population expressing PD-1 and TCF7. Combining abemaciclib with anti-PD-1 produced complete regression in 62 percent of animals versus 8 percent with either agent alone. Depletion of CD8-positive cells abolished the benefit entirely, establishing that the combination effect requires cytotoxic lymphocytes rather than deeper direct growth suppression.

sections.name: Introduction
sections.text: Hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is immunologically quiet, with low mutational burden and sparse lymphocytic infiltrate, and single-agent checkpoint blockade produces responses in fewer than one in ten patients. Any intervention that changes this would apply to the majority of breast cancer patients. Work in xenograft systems has shown that palbociclib drives most estrogen receptor-positive tumor cells into a persistent senescent state with an interleukin 6 and CXCL8 secretory program, and that this reservoir survives through BCL-xL dependence; that study could not address whether the secretory program engages the adaptive immune system because the host lacked one. CDK4 and CDK6 are also expressed in lymphocytes, so the same drug may act on tumor and host in opposite directions, and the balance may depend on schedule.

sections.name: Methods
sections.text: Three transplantable estrogen receptor-positive lines were implanted orthotopically in immunocompetent hosts with estrogen supplementation. Abemaciclib was given at 50 mg/kg daily or on a five-days-on two-days-off schedule. Anti-PD-1 clone RMP1-14 was administered at 200 micrograms every 3 days. Tumors were harvested at days 7, 21, and 42. A 42-parameter mass cytometry panel was applied to barcoded samples, twenty per acquisition. Double-stranded RNA was quantified by J2 antibody dot blot and by strand-specific sequencing of repeat elements. Sorted CD45-positive populations were profiled by indexed droplet transcriptomic sequencing with hashtag multiplexing. CD8 depletion used clone 2.43 beginning 3 days before treatment. Group sizes were ten animals; regression rates were compared by Fisher exact test.

sections.name: Results
sections.text: MHC class I surface abundance rose 3.4-fold by day 7 and remained elevated at day 42. ERV-derived transcripts increased 6.1-fold and cytosolic double-stranded RNA rose in parallel, with IFNL2 and IFNL3 induction of 8.9-fold and 5.2-fold. Senescence markers appeared in 51 percent of tumor cells by day 21. Regulatory T cell Ki-67 positivity fell from 44 to 11 percent while CD8 Ki-67 fell only from 38 to 29 percent. The intermittent schedule produced a higher effector to regulatory ratio than continuous dosing, at 7.8 versus 4.2, and higher complete regression rates in combination, 62 versus 34 percent. CD8 depletion reduced complete regression to 4 percent, and depletion of natural killer cells had no significant effect.

sections.name: Discussion
sections.text: These results indicate that a drug developed as an antiproliferative agent has a substantial immune mechanism that can be exploited by schedule. The superiority of intermittent dosing is consistent with the idea that continuous exposure suppresses the effector expansion that checkpoint blockade requires, and it argues against the reflex assumption that more continuous target coverage is better. Our observation that senescence markers accumulate alongside interferon induction connects the secretory program described in immunodeficient xenograft systems to an adaptive immune consequence that could not be observed there. Clinical translation will require schedules that differ from those approved, since the approved abemaciclib schedule is continuous.
